## MARIANO LENZI
# TO THE VALIANT LADY
## AURELIA PETRUCCI.

*<term>IT WAS</term> an ancient custom of the writ-*
<note>The original text begins with a decorative woodcut "F" (part of the word "FV," meaning "It was"). This letter "F" depicts a scholar in his study, a common motif in Renaissance books to signal the start of a scholarly or philosophical work.</note>
*ers of Egypt to dedicate the most holy books*
*they wrote to Mercury, because*
*they believed that all the arts,*
*all the sciences, and all beautiful things*
*had been discovered by Mercury,*
<note>original: "Mercurio." In the Renaissance, Mercury was identified with Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Egyptian figure thought to be the source of all ancient wisdom (Hermeticism).</note>
*and that to him, as the inventor of everything, it was fit-*
*ting to give thanks for what man learned or knew.*
*And for this reason Pythagoras, Plato, and many other great*
*philosophers went to learn philosophy in Egypt, and for*
*the most part they learned it from the columns of Mercury, which*
<note>The "columns of Mercury" refers to the legendary stelae or pillars on which Hermes Trismegistus was said to have inscribed the totality of human knowledge to preserve it from floods or fire.</note>
*were entirely full of wisdom and doctrine. I similarly,*
*valiant Lady, judge that whatever can be done by*
*those who have known the height of your spirit,*
*is fitting for you; and that their beautiful thoughts, nourished by*
*your divine spirit, ought to return to you, and to the*
*honor of your name, however much they may exert themselves;*
*for it is the case that they learn true virtues no less in the exam-*
*ple of your life than those ancient philosophers*
*did from the columns of Mercury: for, if one considers the nobility,*
*the height, and the gentleness of your spirit;*
*if one regards your honesty, courtesy, and grace; if one*
*considers your prudence, discernment, and wisdom;*
*and finally, if every one of your virtues is admired*
*piece by piece: it is certainly seen by refined minds that there is*
<note>original: "ingegni purgati," literally "purified intellects." This refers to people with the education and moral clarity to recognize true excellence.</note>
*nothing else in our life but a mirror and an Idea of the world...*
<note>The word "Idea" here is used in the Platonic sense—an eternal, perfect pattern or archetype of which physical things are merely shadows.</note>

<summary>In this dedication, Mariano Lenzi compares the noblewoman Aurelia Petrucci to the legendary pillars of Egyptian wisdom, claiming her life serves as a modern monument of virtue for scholars to study.</summary>

->DIALOGUE<-

<meta>catchword: DIA-</meta>

# DIALOGUE

*how it befits others to live; and those who, mired in earthly things, cannot raise themselves in an instant to this celestial thought, provided they turn their eyes toward you, enlightened by your ray, little by little they are purified, and make themselves worthy of the high contemplation of your divinity. Recognizing therefore this common debt, as well as my own, I have acted like those who, being unable to pay from their own resources, pay with what belongs to others; for desiring to discharge part of this great obligation that I have toward you, and through the poverty of my own intellect being unable to send you fruit that was born of myself, I send it to you born in the gardens of others—namely, the books of love by <term>Master Leone</term>, under the titles of <term>Philo</term> and <term>Sophia</term>:*
<note>"Master Leone" refers to Leone Ebreo (Judah Leon Abravanel), a Jewish physician and philosopher. "Philo" and "Sophia" are the two characters in his dialogues; their names are derived from the Greek words for "Love" and "Wisdom," together forming the word "Philosophy."</note>
*a chaste subject of love to a chaste lady who breathes love; celestial thoughts to a lady who is adorned with celestial virtues; the highest understandings to a lady full of the highest concepts. Thus I have chosen to show you my desire to satisfy you with the work of others, rather than prolong, through my poverty <note>original: "pouertà m..." likely "mia," meaning "my poverty."</note>, the satisfaction of so great a debt. However, I judge (whenever I think of it) that I make two no small gains at once: to discharge part of this obligation to you, and to place under obligation to me (if shadows can be obligated) <term>Master Leone</term>. For since I have drawn these divine dialogues of his out of the shadows in which they lay buried, and placed them as if into clear light, and recommended them to the name of so valiant a lady as you are, I believe for certain that he must be supremely gladdened by it—both for this new splendor of his, and for such high protection—and must remain much obligated to me.*
<note>Leone Ebreo died roughly a decade before this edition was published; Lenzi refers to him as a "shadow" or "shade," suggesting that by publishing the work, he is doing a service to the deceased author's legacy.</note>
*You, therefore, having become as it were the guardian of this work, by directing toward it—as into a body most fit to receive light—your ray, you will make it more splendid and cause it to appear more miraculous to the world.*

<summary>In this dedication, Mariano Lenzi presents Leone Ebreo's "Dialogues of Love" to Aurelia Petrucci, framing the publication as a way to honor both the patroness and the deceased author. He uses Neoplatonic metaphors of light and purification to describe Petrucci's influence on the text and its readers.</summary>
<keywords>Mariano Lenzi, Aurelia Petrucci, Leone Ebreo, Philo, Sophia, Neoplatonism, Renaissance philosophy, patronage, Dialoghi d'amore</keywords>

->DIALOGUE<-

# FIRST DIALOGUE ON LOVE,
## BY LEONE EBREO

### I N T E R L O C U T O R S:
### PHILO AND SOPHIA.

->PHILO.<-

<margin>
A most noble... speaks of a love and desire...
</margin>

**T**o know you, O Sophia, causes in me love and desire. <note>Philo and Sophia represent the two halves of 'Philosophy': *Philo* (Love) and *Sophia* (Wisdom).</note> SOPHIA: These feelings that the knowledge of me produces in you seem discordant to me, O Philo; but perhaps passion makes you say so. PHILO: They discord with yours, which are far from any correspondence. SOPHIA: Rather, loving and desiring are, in themselves, contrary <term>affects of the will</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "affects of the will" refers to the ways the soul is moved or inclined toward an object.</note>. PHILO: And why contrary? SOPHIA: Because those things we deem good, which we have and possess, we love; and those which we lack, we desire; so that what is loved is first desired, and after the desired thing is obtained, love comes and desire ceases. PHILO: What moves you to hold this opinion? SOPHIA: The example of things that are loved and desired. Do you not see that health, when we do not have it, we desire? But we would not yet say we love it. And once we have it, we love it, and no longer desire it. Riches, inheritances, and jewels, before they are possessed, are desired and not loved; after they are obtained, they are no longer desired, but loved. PHILO: Although health and riches, when they are lacking, cannot be loved because we do not have them, nevertheless one loves the *having* of them. SOPHIA: This is an improper way of speaking—to say "loving," meaning "wanting"...

<sig>A 3</sig>

<summary>This page opens the famous philosophical dialogue between Philo and Sophia, beginning with a debate on the definitions of love and desire. Sophia argues that desire is for what we lack, while love is for what we already possess, using health and wealth as examples.</summary>
<keywords>Philo, Sophia, Leone Ebreo, Love, Desire, Philosophy, Renaissance Neoplatonism, Affects of the Will</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the opening dialogue between Philo and Sophia from Leone Ebreo’s "Dialogues of Love." Following the introduction of the characters, they are now engaged in a philosophical debate over whether love and desire can exist at the same time for the same object.</meta>

->DIALOGUE<-

*...to possess the thing, which is to say one desires it: because love is for the actual thing loved, and desire is for the having or the acquiring of it; nor does it seem possible for loving and desiring to exist together.* <note>Sophia argues that love and desire are mutually exclusive: you desire what you lack and love what you already have.</note> **Ph.** *Your arguments, O Sophia, demonstrate the subtlety of your intellect more than the truth of your opinion: for if we do not love that which we desire, we would be desiring that which is not loved; and consequently that which is abhorred and hated; there could be no greater contradiction.* **So.** *I am not mistaken, O Philo: for I desire that which—though I do not love it now because I do not possess it—will be loved by me once I have it, and no longer desired. Nor do I ever desire what I abhor, nor yet what I already love: because the thing loved is held, and the thing desired is lacking. And what clearer example can be given than that of children? He who does not have them cannot love them, but desires them; and he who has them does not desire them, but loves them.* **Ph.** *Just as you show by the example of children, you should remember the husband: who, before he is had, is desired and loved at the same time; and after he is had, desire fails, and sometimes love as well, although in many cases it not only perseveres but even grows. This often happens similarly to the husband regarding the wife. Does this example not seem more sufficient to confirm my statement than yours to disprove it?* **So.** *This talk of yours satisfies me in part, but not entirely, especially following your example which is similar to the doubt we are debating.* **Ph.** *I will speak to you more generally. You know that love is for things that are good, or esteemed as good: because any good thing is lovable; and just as there are three kinds of good: the <term>profitable</term> <note>Philo is introducing the classic Aristotelian division of "The Good" into three categories: the Profitable (useful), the Pleasurable (delightful), and the Honest (virtuous/moral).</note>,*

<meta>catchword: uole, [profitable]</meta>

<summary>Philo and Sophia debate whether love and desire can coexist, with Sophia arguing they are sequential (desire ends when possession/love begins) while Philo argues they must overlap, using marriage as a counter-example.</summary>
<keywords>Leone Ebreo, Philo, Sophia, philosophy of love, desire vs love, Renaissance Platonism, three kinds of good</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue between Philo (Filone) and Sophia from the First Dialogue of Leone Ebreo's "Dialogues of Love." Philo is currently explaining the Aristotelian categories of the "Good" (useful, pleasant, and virtuous) to argue that love and desire are not mutually exclusive.</meta>

->FIRST<-

<margin>Three types of Love</margin>
[use]ful, pleasant, and virtuous; so too are there three types of love: one is the pleasant, the other the useful, and the other the virtuous. Of these, the latter two, when they are possessed at any time, must be loved, either before they are acquired or afterward. The pleasant <note>Italian: *dilettabile*; referring to things that satisfy the physical senses</note> is not loved after it is obtained; for all things that delight our material senses, by their nature, once they are possessed, are more quickly abhorred than loved. It is necessary, therefore, for this reason, that you concede that such things are loved before they are possessed, and likewise when they are desired. But because after they are entirely possessed, desire fails, the love of them also fails most of the time. For this reason, you must concede that love and desire can exist together.

**So.** Your reasons, in my judgment, have the power to prove that first statement of yours; but mine, which are contrary to it, are not for that reason weak, nor stripped of truth. How is it possible, then, for one truth to be contrary to the same truth? Resolve this ambiguity for me, which leaves me quite confused.

**Ph.** <note>Original: *FI.* for Filone. In the tradition of the text, Philo represents the lover/philosopher and Sophia represents wisdom/the beloved.</note> I come, O Sophia, to ask you for a remedy for my pains, and you ask me for the solution to your doubts; perhaps you do it to divert me from this pursuit <note>original: *prattica*, referring here to his romantic suit or the current conversation</note>, which does not please you, or perhaps because the concepts of my poor intellect displease you no less than the affections of my troubled will.

**So.** I cannot deny that the sweet and pure mind has more power to move me than does the amorous will. Nor do I believe I do you an injury by this, esteeming in you that which is of greater value; for if you love me, as you say, you ought sooner to seek to quiet my intellect than to in— <note>The text breaks off mid-word as the dialogue continues on the following page.</note>

<summary>Philo argues that love and desire can coexist, especially regarding sensory pleasures that are desired before they are had but often loathed once possessed. Sophia, confused by how two opposing logical arguments can both seem true, asks Philo to prioritize satisfying her intellectual curiosity over his romantic desires.</summary>

<keywords>pleasant love, useful love, virtuous love, desire vs. possession, Philo, Sophia, Neoplatonism, 16th-century philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the First Dialogue of Leone Ebreo’s "Dialogues of Love" (Dialoghi d'Amore). In the previous section, Philo (Filone) began to explain that love and desire can coexist by categorizing the "Good" into the useful, the pleasant, and the virtuous. Here, Sophia (Wisdom) challenges him to resolve the logical contradiction between loving what one already has and desiring what one lacks.</meta>

# D I A L O G U E

<meta>catchword: FI.</meta>

->+<-

...whet my appetite: so that, putting all other things aside, you might resolve these doubts of mine. 

**Ph.** <note>original: *FI.* for Filone, the character representing the lover and the seeker of knowledge.</note> Even though the contrary argument is ready at hand, I must nevertheless follow your will by force; this comes from the law that beloved victors <note>original: *uincitori amati*; a metaphor for the beloved's power over the lover's mind</note> have imposed upon those they have forced and conquered as lovers. I say that there are some who hold an opinion entirely contrary to yours: they maintain that love and desire are, in effect, one and the same thing, because they claim that everything one desires, one also loves. 

**So.** <note>original: *SO.* for Sophia, the character representing wisdom and the object of Philo's affection.</note> They are clearly in error; for even if one grants them that everything desired is loved, it is certain that many things are loved which are not desired—as is the case with all things already possessed. 

**Ph.** You have argued against them correctly. But some others believe that love is a certain thing that contains within itself all things desired (even if they are not yet possessed) and similarly those good things already acquired and held, which are no longer desired. 

**So.** This does not yet resolve my confusion: because (as the saying goes) many things are desired which cannot be loved, because they do not have being <note>original: *in essere*; referring to existence in reality versus potentiality</note>. Love is of things that *are*, and desire is proper to those things that *are not*. How can we love children or health if we do not have them, even if we desire them? This makes me hold that love and desire are two contrary affections <note>original: *affetti*; used here to mean "dispositions" or "movements" of the soul</note> of the will. Yet you told me that both can exist together. Clarify this doubt for me. 

**Ph.** If love is only for things that have being, why should desire not also be for them? 

**So.** Because, just as love presupposes the being of things, so desire presupposes the privation <note>original: *priuatione*; a technical philosophical term from Aristotle meaning the lack or absence of a quality that should naturally be present</note> of them.

**love, desire, will, contraries, privation, appetite, beloved victors, conquered lovers**

<summary>Sophia argues that love and desire must be opposites because love requires the presence of an object while desire requires its absence. Philo begins to challenge this distinction by questioning why desire cannot also apply to things that exist.</summary>
<keywords>love vs desire, being and privation, philosophy of will, Neoplatonism, Leone Ebreo, beloved victor, conquered lover</keywords>

# FIRST [DIALOGUE]

<meta>The catchword 'rarla' from the previous page likely refers to 'parlarla' (to speak of it), continuing the dialogue where Sophia asks Philo to resolve her doubts.</meta>

->+<-

...speak of it: so that, putting all other things aside, you might resolve these doubts of mine.

**Ph.** <note>original: *FI.*, abbreviation for Filone (Philo)</note> *For what reason does love presuppose the being <term>being: *essere*; in this context, it refers to actual existence or the state of being real</term> of things?*
<margin>how knowledge <gloss>recognition</gloss> precedes love</margin>
**So.** <note>original: *SO.*, abbreviation for Sofia (Sophia)</note> *Because it is necessary that knowledge precedes love: for no thing could be loved, if first it were not known under the appearance of something good; and nothing falls within our knowledge, if it is not first actually found to be in existence. For our mind is a mirror and an exemplar <note>original: *essempio*; meaning a model or pattern that reflects reality</note>—or to put it better, an image of real things—in such a way that there is nothing that can be loved if it is not first found to be really in existence.* **Ph.** *You speak the truth; but for this same reason, desire cannot apply except to things that have being: because we do not desire anything except those things that we first know under the appearance of being good. For this reason, the Philosopher <note>A standard Renaissance reference to Aristotle, specifically his Nicomachean Ethics</note> has defined the Good as that which everyone desires, since knowledge is of things that have being.* **So.** *It cannot be denied that knowledge precedes desire; but I would say instead that not only is every cognition <note>The process of knowing or perceiving</note> of things that are, but also of those that are not. For our intellect judges a thing that is, just as it judges it; and likewise another that is not. And since its office <note>its duty or function</note> is to discern between the being of things and their non-being, it must know both those that are and those that are not. I would say, then, that love presupposes the cognition of things that are, and desire [presupposes the cognition] of those things that are not, and of those things which we lack.* **Ph.** *To love, just as much as to desire, the knowledge of the thing loved or desired precedes [the act], which [knowledge] is good. And for neither of them should the cognition be anything but good: because such a cognition would be the cause of making one totally abhor the known thing, and not desire—*

<summary>Sophia and Philo debate whether love and desire require the object to actually exist, concluding that while love is for what exists, desire is for what we lack or what does not yet exist.</summary>
<keywords>Philo, Sophia, love vs desire, epistemology, Aristotle, being and non-being, cognition, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the First Dialogue of Leone Ebreo’s "Dialogues of Love." Following the previous page, Sophia and Philo are debating whether love and desire require the object of that affection to actually exist ("to have being"). # DIALOGUE

->+<-

...to speak of it, or to love it; so that love, just like desire, equally presupposes the being <term>being: *essere*; the state of existence or reality</term> of things, as much in reality as in our knowledge.

**So.** <note>Sophia, whose name means "Wisdom" in Greek</note> If desire presupposed the being of things, it would follow that whenever we judge a thing to be good and desirable, such a judgment would always be true. But do you not see that many times this judgment is false, and the thing is not actually found to be so in reality? It would seem, then, that desire does not always presuppose the being of the thing desired.

Thus, the one, like the other, presupposes the being of the thing <note>Philo argues that even if we are wrong about a thing's quality, we still react to it as if it truly exists in that form</note>.

**Ph.** We indeed always desire what we do not have, but not for that reason do we desire what does not exist. On the contrary, desire is usually for things that *are*, but which we cannot possess.

**So.** Yet desire is also for those things that effectively are not, and we well desire that they might be, though we do not necessarily desire to possess them. For example: we desire that it rain when it is not raining; and that there be good weather; and that a friend arrives; and that something be accomplished. And as for those things you mentioned, even if they do not exist in a present, actual state <term>actual being: *essere attuale*; existence as a completed fact in the world</term> at the moment they are desired, their being is nonetheless possible <term>possible being: *essere possibile*; the capacity or potential for something to exist</term>. And because of this possible being, one can still desire that they might pass into actual being—just as those things which already exist but which we do not yet have can be desired so that we might possess them. Thus, every desire is either that something which does not yet exist should come into being, or that we might have what we currently lack. Why, then, do you insist that every desire presupposes being in part and privation <term>privation: *priuatione*; a philosophical term for the absence of a quality or state that should naturally exist</term> in part, and that it seeks the fulfillment of being which it lacks? It follows that desire and love are founded upon the being of a thing, and not upon its non-existence. Indeed, three "titles" or qualities must precede a desirable thing in this specific order: the first is being, the second is truth, and the third is that it be good. Only with these does it come to be loved and desired. This could not happen if the thing were not first esteemed as good, for otherwise, it would be neither loved nor desired. And before it is judged to be good, it must be known as true; and because it actually exists before it is known, it must first possess real being. For first the thing exists in being, then it is impressed upon the intellect, then it is judged to be good, and finally, it is loved and desired. This is why the Philosopher <note>A common medieval and Renaissance reference to Aristotle</note> says that being, truth, and goodness are convertible <note>original: *si conuertono*; a scholastic concept where "Being," "Truth," and "Goodness" are different names for the same reality</note> into one another; except that "being" refers to the thing in itself, "truth" is when it is impressed upon the intellect, and "goodness" is when it moves from the intellect and the will toward the

For such loves, when stripped of reason, are evil and vicious, and belong more to brute animals than to humans. And the middle path that reason establishes in this is the only true love; and from that middle path it is verified that the more excessively one desires, loves, and follows it, the more truly it is virtue. This is because such a desire is no longer mere pleasure or utility, but depends on the moderation of those things, which is an intellectual virtue, and truly an honorable thing.*

-tuous, <note>Completing the word from the previous page: "virtuoso."</note> honor, fame, and glory—which are all things that are loved and desired—it is not clearly manifest whether they belong to the category of the useful, or the pleasurable, or indeed the honorable. <note>original: "honesto" – referring to things that are morally good in themselves.</note> For while in one respect they appear pleasurable because of the delight achieved in possessing them, on the other hand it seems they are not, because once they are had and possessed, they are still loved without ever reaching satiety and distaste. <note>original: "fastidio" – a sense of weariness or cloying boredom that comes from having too much of a simple pleasure.</note> This would suggest they belong to the category of useful and honorable things rather than the pleasurable. <margin>What kind of love the love of health is:</margin> <term>FI.</term> <note>Philo, the male speaker in the dialogue.</note> Although health achieves what is useful, its specific nature belongs to the pleasurable. Health, therefore, principally possesses a pleasure suited to its own delight. It is not only useful, but also honorable, and for this reason, possessing it to the full is not wearisome, nor does it ever become a cause of distaste like other purely pleasurable things, which are not valued when they are possessed as much as they are desired when they are lacking. 

There is also another reason why one does not grow weary of health, nor does it become a distasteful burden: because the feeling of its delight is not restricted to the external material senses—such as taste in the case of food, or touch in the case of carnal pleasure, or smell in the case of scents (all of which quickly lead to distaste)—but it also belongs to the spiritual senses, <note>In Renaissance philosophy, sight and hearing were considered "spiritual" or "higher" senses because they can perceive beauty and harmony from a distance without physical consumption.</note> which are much slower to reach satiety. This is not because health consists in hearing, like sweet harmonies and soft voices, nor in seeing, like beautiful and well-proportioned figures; rather, the delight of health is felt through the entire human sentiment, both the exterior and interior senses, and an-

<summary>Philo explains that health is a unique form of pleasure because it is also "honorable" and "useful," meaning it does not lead to the boredom or distaste that typically follows the overindulgence of physical senses.</summary>

<margin>
The effects of true friendship
</margin>
belonging to each of them is common to both. Sometimes the good delights the friend more, and the ill saddens him more, than it does the person actually experiencing it; and often a person takes on a portion of their friend's troubles to lighten them, or truly to help them through friendship in their labors—for companionship in tribulations causes them to be felt less.

<margin>
The definition of friendship
</margin>
And the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>original: "il filosofo"; a standard Renaissance reference to Aristotle, who discussed friendship extensively in his Nicomachean Ethics</note> defines such friendships by saying that the true friend is "another self." This is to denote that whoever exists in true friendship has a double life constituted in two people: in their own and in that of the friend. Thus, his friend is "another self," and each of them embraces two lives within themselves—their own and their friend’s—and with equal love, they love both persons and likewise preserve both lives. For this reason, <term>Holy Scripture</term> commands honorable friendship, saying:
> You shall love your neighbor as yourself. <note>original: "Amarai il prossimo come te medesimo"; a reference to the biblical commandment found in Leviticus 19:18</note>
It intends for friendship to be of such a nature that the two become equally united, and that one and the same love exists in the soul of each friend.

<margin>
The causes that must concur to form true friendship
</margin>
And the cause of such union and binding is the reciprocal virtue or wisdom of both friends. Because of its spirituality, its detachment from matter, and its abstraction from bodily conditions, this virtue removes the diversity of persons that arises from physical individuality; it generates within the friends a single <term>mental essence</term> <note>original: "essentia mentale"; the idea that the minds of two friends merge into a single intellectual reality</note> preserved...

Nor is our will capable of such an excessive love. Rather, it is the role of our mind to know according to its own possibility of knowing, and not according to the immense excellence of the thing being known. Nor does our will love Him according to how worthy He is of being loved, but only as far as our will can extend itself toward Him in the act of loving. **SO.** But can a thing truly be known if it is not fully comprehended by the one who knows it? **FI.** It is enough that the part of the thing which is known is comprehended. For the thing known is always grasped by the knower according to the power of the knower, and not according to the power of the thing known. Do you not see that the form of a man is imprinted and captured in a mirror, not according to the perfect human essence, but according to the capacity and quality of the mirror’s perfection—which is only figurative and not essential? Fire is perceived by the eye not according to its burning nature—for if it were so, it would burn the eye—but only according to its color and shape. And what greater...

-># B O O K   O N E<-

...example that the great hemisphere <term>hemisphere: here referring to the visible vault of the heavens</term> of the sky could be understood by so small a part as the eye? See how great its smallness is, that some wise man may be found who believes it to be indivisible, incapable of receiving any natural division. Therefore, the eye understands things according to its own visual power, its size, and its nature, but not according to the condition of the things seen in themselves. And in this manner, our small intellect perceives the infinite God according to human capacity and intelligible power, but not according to the bottomless sea <note>original: "pelago"; a poetic term for a great depth or abyss of water</note> of the divine essence and immense wisdom. To this knowledge, the love of God serves and responds according to the ability of the human will, but it is not proportionate to the infinite goodness of that most perfect God.

**SO.** <note>Sofia, the seeker of wisdom</note> Tell me, is desire mixed into this love of God?

**FI.** <note>Filone, the lover of wisdom</note> On the contrary, divine love is never stripped of ardent desire; this desire is to acquire that which is lacking in one's knowledge of the divine. In this way, as knowledge grows, the love of the known Divinity also grows. Because the divine essence exceeds human knowledge by an infinite proportion—and His goodness no less exceeds the love that humans bear Him—there remains to man (who is nonetheless happy) a most ardent and unrestrained desire to always increase his knowledge and love of the divine. Of this increase, man always has the possibility because of the nature of the Object being known and loved; although on man's own part, it may be that such effects are fixed at a certain degree beyond which he cannot advance. Or perhaps, even after reaching the highest degree, there remains in him an impression of desire to know what he lacks without ever being able to reach it, even though he has attained a state of bliss <term>bliss: "beatitudine"; the ultimate state of spiritual happiness and union with God</term>.

Opinions
regarding

**S O.** Since we have come to this, I would like to know in what way this human beatitude consists. **F I.** Diverse have been the opinions of men on the subject of happiness. Many have placed it in utility, and the possession of the goods of fortune, and the abundance of those things as long as life lasts. But the falsity of this opinion is manifest: because such exterior goods are caused by interior ones, in such a way that the former depend on the latter, and happiness must consist in the most excellent things. Furthermore, this happiness is the end <term>end: the 'telos' or ultimate goal and purpose</term> of the others, and not for any other end, but all others exist for this; especially since such exterior goods are in the power of fortune, and happiness must be in the power of man. Some others have held a different opinion, saying that beatitude consists in the pleasurable: and these are the Epicureans <note>followers of Epicurus, often characterized in this period as seeking only physical or temporal pleasure</note>, who hold the mortality of the soul, and believe nothing in man to be happy except pleasure in whatever manner it may be. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Sofia and Filone. Having previously discussed the nature of human happiness (beatitude) and why the soul seeks God, Filone now begins to categorize the specific "habits" or intellectual dispositions that elevate humans above animals.</meta>

-># FIRST #<-

...and in the acts and habits of the intellectual soul, which are the most excellent and the goal of all other human habits; it is through these that man is human, possessing greater excellence than any other animal.

<margin>five habits of the intellectual acts</margin>
**S O.** How many, and of what kind, are these habits of the intellectual acts? **F I.** I say there are five: Art, Prudence, Intellect, Science, and Wisdom.

<margin>What art is</margin>
**S O.** In what way do you define them? **F I.** Art is the habit of things to be made according to reason; these are things made with the hands and through bodily labor. Within this habit are included all the mechanical arts <note>In the Renaissance, "mechanical arts" referred to manual trades like weaving, agriculture, or masonry, often contrasted with the "liberal arts."</note> in which a physical instrument is used.

<margin>what Prudence is</margin>
Prudence is the habit of acts to be performed <term>performed: 'agibili,' referring to moral conduct and practical ethics rather than the making of physical objects</term> according to reason. It consists in the practice of good human customs, and within this are included all the virtues that operate through the will and the voluntary effects of love and desire.

<margin>what the intellect is</margin>
The intellect is the principle of knowing. These habits <note>Here, Filone refers to self-evident truths or first principles.</note> are known and accepted by everyone naturally once the terms are understood—such as the principle that good should be sought and evil avoided, that contraries cannot exist together at the same time, and other similar truths. In these, the intellectual power operates in its first state of being.

<margin>Definition of science</margin>
Science is the habit of knowledge and conclusion which is generated from the aforementioned principles. Within this are included the seven liberal arts <note>The "seven liberal arts" comprised the Trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and the Quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy).</note>; in this, the intellect operates in the middle of its being.

<margin>what Wisdom is</margin>
Wisdom is the habit of both of these together—that is, of both the principle and the conclusion of all things that have being. This alone reaches the highest knowledge of spiritual things; the Greeks call it theology <note>original: "theologia"</note>, which means divine science; and it is called first philosophy...

...these two more than any of the other **senses** <term>senses</term> <note>original: "sentimenti"; in this philosophical context, it refers to the five physical senses.</note>, which are seeing, hearing, and smelling. The reason for this is that these three are not necessary for the individual existence of man, nor for the **succession of the species** <note>original: "successione della spetie"; the continuation of the human race through reproduction.</note>; rather, they exist solely for the convenience and utility of human beings and the perfect animals. Therefore, just as their existence is not strictly necessary, they have no need of boundaries or limitations in their operation. 

And just as not seeing, not hearing, and not smelling does not deprive a man of his life, so too he is not deprived of life by superfluous seeing, superfluous hearing, or frequent smelling—unless it should happen by accident. But with **taste** and **touch**, just as their existence is necessary for human life and succession (so much so that if they were absent, life would be lost), so too their excess would be the cause of man's **deprivation** <note>original: "priuazione"; meaning the destruction or death of the individual.</note>. 

For eating and drinking too much would kill a man no less than hunger and thirst. Likewise, frequent **carnal union** <note>original: "copula carnale"; sexual intercourse.</note> and excessive heat or cold affecting the touch would be the cause of his corruption. Since these two senses act as a bond of greater **delight** <note>original: "dilettatione"; physical pleasure.</note> because of their necessity for man’s own being and that of his successors, it is necessary to limit them naturally. This is so that even if delight should transport them toward a harmful excess, the natural limit might restrain them, so that such excess cannot destroy the individual. 

In this way, **nature** has shown no less wisdom in placing a natural limit and restraint upon the senses of taste and touch for man's preservation than she showed in producing them for his very existence. And although the appetite of the lover is satisfied through carnal union, and that desire—or rather, appetite—continually ceases, it does not p... <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "questa" suggests the next sentence begins with "this."</note>

# -> BOOK ONE <-

...likely, rather than subtle; I judge from experience, which must be believed more than any other reason. We see many who love, and once they have obtained from their beloved that which they desire of bodily acts of love, not only does their desire cease, but their love vanishes entirely, and sometimes even turns to hate. Such was the case with **Amnon** <note>original: "Amone"; Amnon, the eldest son of King David.</note>, son of David, who loved **Tamar** <note>original: "Athamar"; Tamar, Amnon's half-sister. The story is found in 2 Samuel 13.</note> his sister with such intensity that he had become ill and was in danger of death because of it; and after **Jonadab** <note>original: "Ionadab"; a cousin and advisor to Amnon who devised the plan to trap Tamar.</note> with deception and violence enabled him to obtain what he desired from her, he immediately felt such hatred for her that he made her leave his house in the middle of the day in her violated state.

<margin>Two kinds of Love</margin>
*FI.* Love is of two kinds. One generates desire, or rather <term>sensual appetite</term> <note>original: "appetito sensuale"; physical cravings associated with the lower senses as opposed to intellectual or spiritual longing.</note>, such that when a person desires someone, they love them. This love is imperfect because it depends on a flawed and fragile principle, being a child born of desire. Such was the love of Amnon toward Tamar; and it is true, as you say, that when the carnal desire or appetite ceases through its satisfaction and **satiety** <note>original: "satietà"; the state of being fed or gratified beyond the point of desire.</note>, the love immediately ceases entirely. This is because when the cause—which is desire—ceases, the effect—which is love—also ceases; and many times it turns into hatred, as happened in that case. 

But the other love is that from which the desire for the beloved person is generated, rather than being born from desire or appetite. Instead, by loving perfectly first, the force of love makes one desire spiritual and corporal union with the beloved person. Thus, just as the first kind of love is the child of desire, so this love is the father and true generator of desire. **SO.** Be it as you wish; I forgive your forgetfulness, but not the promise. And since we have an opportune time, let us sit under this shade, and tell me of the birth of love, and what was its first origin.

**FI.** If you wish for us to speak of the birth of love, it will be necessary in this present <term>confabulation</term> <note>original: "confabulatione." In this context, it refers to a formal philosophical discussion or dialogue.</note> first to tell you of the commonality of its being and of its ample universality; and at another time we shall speak of its birth.

**SO.** Is not the origin of a thing prior to its universality?

**FI.** It is indeed prior in being, but it is not prior in our <term>cognition</term> <note>original: "cognitione." This refers to the human process of understanding or perceiving reality.</note>.

**SO.** How so?

**FI.** Because the commonality of love is more manifest to us than its origin, and from known things one comes to the knowledge of unknown things.

**SO.** You truly speak the truth, for the universality of love is quite manifest; since almost no human is devoid of it, neither male nor female, nor old nor young; and even infants in their first cognition love their mothers and their nurses.

**FI.** Do you not know, then, of love more common than the human race?

**SO.** Love is also found in all irrational animals that <term>generate</term> <note>original: "generano." Referring to the biological act of procreation and the instincts associated with it.</note>, between females and males, and between offspring and parents.

**FI.** Not only is generation the cause of the love found in humans and other animals, but there are many other factors; nevertheless, love...

# -> D I A L O G U E <-

<margin>
Two causes of Love that humans have [which differ] from those of animals.
</margin>

...of which animals are totally deprived.

**SO.** Explain them to me.

**FI.** The first is the conformity of nature and <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "complessione." In Renaissance medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual.</note> of one human with another. Without any other apparent reason, upon their first meeting, this causes them to become friends; and finding no other cause for such friendship, it is said that their temperaments are compatible. In effect, it is a certain similarity or harmonic correspondence of one temperament to another. Likewise, one also finds hatred among men without an apparent cause, which derives from a disproportionate dissimilarity of their temperaments. The <term>astrologers</term> <note>In the 16th century, astrology was considered a serious science used to explain human behavior and health.</note> say that this friendly conformity proceeds from a similar or proportional position of the planets and celestial signs in the <term>nativity</term> <note>An astrological birth chart.</note> of both individuals; just as the hostile difference in temperaments derives from a dissimilar and disproportionate celestial position at their births. This cause of love and friendship we recognize in humans, but not in animals.

**SO.** What is the other?

**FI.** The other consists of the moral and intellectual virtues. These are the qualities for which excellent men are greatly loved by good men, and the merit of these virtues causes <term>noble love</term> <note>original: "amore honesto." This refers to a high-minded, virtuous love based on the appreciation of the soul and character, rather than physical desire (the "pleasant") or personal gain (the "useful").</note>, which is the most worthy of all. For human persons, without any other cause and solely for virtue and wisdom, love one another effectively with a love more perfect and firm than that based on the useful or the pleasant—in which two categories all the other five causes of love are included. This alone is noble love; it is generated by right reason, and for this reason, it is not found in irrational animals.

**SO.** I have understood how many causes of love there are in humans and in irrational animals, but I see that all of them belong to living beings, and...

## -> SECOND DIALOGUE <-

...none [of these causes] apply to non-living bodies, and yet you still say that love is not only common to animals, but also to other inanimate bodies; this seems strange to me.

**FI.** Why strange? 

**SO.** Because nothing can be loved if it is not first known, and inanimate bodies do not have within themselves the <term>cognitive power</term> <note>The capacity to perceive, recognize, or understand information from the world.</note>. Furthermore, love proceeds from will, or appetite, and is imprinted in the senses: inanimate bodies have neither will, nor appetite, nor senses. How, then, can they possess love?

<margin>Three kinds of knowledge, appetite, and Love</margin>

**FI.** Knowledge, appetite, and consequently love, exist in three modes: natural, sensitive, and rational-voluntary.

**SO.** Explain all three to me. 

**FI.** Natural knowledge, appetite, or love is that which is found in non-sensing bodies, such as the <term>elements</term> <note>Earth, Water, Air, and Fire—the four basic building blocks of the universe in Renaissance science.</note> and the bodies composed of those inanimate elements, such as metals and types of stones, and even plants, herbs, or trees. All of these have a natural knowledge of their <term>end</term> <note>original: "fine." In this context, it refers to a "final cause" or purpose—the natural goal toward which a thing moves.</note> and a natural inclination toward it. This inclination moves them toward that goal, just as heavy bodies are moved to descend to the bottom, and light ones to ascend to the top, as if to a place known and desired as their own. These inclinations I call—and truly they are—natural appetite and love. 

Sensitive knowledge and appetite (or love) is that which is found in irrational animals. It leads them to seek what is suitable for them and flee what is unsuitable—such as seeking food, drink, the right temperature, mating, rest, and similar things. These things must first be known, then desired or loved, and afterwards pursued. For if the animal did not know them, it would not desire them nor love them; and if it did not have the appetite for them, it would not pursue them to obtain them; and not having...

<summary>Sophia questions how inanimate objects can experience love. Philo explains that love exists on three levels—natural, sensitive, and rational—and that even "mindless" objects like stones or fire have a "natural love" that draws them toward their proper place in the universe.</summary>

# DIALOGUE

*...lower [bodies] are rightly directed to know their <term>end</term> <note>original: "fine." In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the "final cause" or the ultimate purpose and natural goal of an object.</note> and their proper places; so they are directed by that [the world soul] to love them, and desire them, and to move themselves to find them when they are separated from them. And just as the arrow seeks the target directly, not through its own knowledge, but through the knowledge of the archer by whom it is directed, so these lower bodies seek their own place and end—not through their own knowledge, but through the correct knowledge of the first creator infused into the <term>world soul</term> <note>The "Anima Mundi," an intrinsic spirit or force believed by many ancient and Renaissance philosophers to animate all nature as if the universe were a single living organism.</note> and into the universal nature of lower things. In this way, just as the inclination of the arrow comes from artificial knowledge, love, or appetite, so the inclination of these irrational bodies comes from natural knowledge and love.* **SO.** *This manner of love and knowledge found in these dead bodies resonates with me; but I would like to know if perhaps another love or appetite is found in them, besides that which they have for their proper places—like light things for the heights and heavy things for the depths.* **FI.** *The love that the <term>elements</term> <note>Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> and other dead bodies have for their proper places, and the hate they have for their opposites, is like the love that animals have for suitable things and the hate they have for unsuitable ones; and so they flee the one and follow the other. This love is also of the same kind as that which terrestrial animals have for the land, marine animals for the water, birds for the air, and the <term>Salamander</term> <note>A mythical lizard-like creature believed in the Renaissance to live in and eat fire.</note> for the fire, which is said to be born in it and to dwell within it. Such is the love of the elements for their proper places. Beyond this kind of love, I tell you that in the elements are found all the other five causes of <term>reciprocal love</term> <note>Love that is mutual or returned; an attraction between two things based on shared qualities.</note> that we said are found in animals.* **SO.** *All of those?* **FI.** *All.*

<margin>
Love of lower things for their own kind

In Renaissance natural philosophy, this refers to an object’s natural kind or category; for example, a stone belongs to the "species" of Earth.</note>, because it is more manifest. You will see that the parts of the earth that find themselves outside of the whole move with an effective love to unite with the entire earth; and thus the stones that congeal in the air quickly seek the earth. And the rivers and other waters generated from exhaling vapors in the cavities of the earth—which then convert into water—as soon as they find themselves in sufficient quantity, they run to find the sea and the whole <term>element</term> <note>Earth, Water, Air, and Fire were considered the four building blocks of the universe.</note> of water because of the love they have for their kind. *...potentially and generatively are in her together, and in a state of confusion <note>In this context, "confusion" refers to the original chaotic state where all possibilities exist but are not yet distinct.</note>, and from her each one is made individually, diffusely, and successively.* **SO.** *And can love fall into such a thing as this?* **FI.** *This <term>prime matter: the fundamental, formless "stuff" of the universe that underlies all physical objects</term>, as Plato says, appetites and loves all the forms of generated things, just as the woman loves the man. And since the actual presence of one of these forms does not satisfy her love, her appetite, or her desire, she falls in love with another form that she lacks; and leaving the former, she takes up the latter. In this way, because she cannot hold all forms together in act <note>original: "in atto." In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" or "actuality" is the finished, realized state of a thing, as opposed to its "potential."</note>, she receives them all successively, one after the other. Furthermore, she possesses all forms together in many of her various parts; but because each of those parts wishes to enjoy the love of all forms, it is necessary for them to be continually transmuted from one into the other. This is because one single form is not enough to satiate her appetite and love, which far exceeds any single satisfaction; for one form alone among these cannot satisfy this insatiable appetite of hers. And just as she is the cause of the continuous generation of those forms she lacks, so she herself is the cause of the continuous corruption <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "corruption" simply means the breaking down or ending of a form, the opposite of "generation."</note> of the forms she already possesses. For this reason, some call her a prostitute <note>original: "meretrice." This is a classical philosophical metaphor (found in Aristotle and later Neoplatonists) to describe how matter "cheats" on one form to embrace another.</note> for not having a single or firm love for one; rather, when she has one, she desires to leave it for another. Yet, through this "adulterous" love, the lower world is adorned with such great and marvelous diversity of things so beautifully formed. Thus, the generative love of this prime matter, and her constant desire for the new husband <note>Here, "husband" refers to a new "form" or "soul" to give the matter shape.</note> that she lacks, and the delight she receives from new intercourse <note>original: "coito"</note>, is the cause of the generation of all things capable of being generated.* **SO.** *I well understand the love, appetite, and insatiable desire that alw...*

<margin>The love of the elements is the generative cause of mixed and composite things.</margin>
**FI.** The love that is usually found in the four elements—even though they are opposites of one another—is the generative cause of all things mixed and composed from them.

**SO.** Explain to me in what manner.

**FI.** The elements are divided and separated because of their contrariety: because fire and air are hot and light, they seek the heights and flee the depths; and because earth and water are cold and heavy, they seek the depths and flee the heights. Yet, many times, through the intercession of the benign heaven, by means of its motion and its rays, they are joined in friendship. In such a form they mix together, and with such friendship, that they arrive almost at a unity of uniform body and uniform quality. This friendship is capable of receiving—through the <term>power of heaven</term><note>The Italian 'virtù del cielo' refers to the specialized influence or "virtue" that celestial bodies exert over earthly matter.</note>—other forms much more excellent than any of the individual elements in their various degrees, while the elements themselves remain there materially mixed.

It also seemed to him that heaven caused a greater and more excellent generation in the lower beings of that part of the earth than in the other. He called the other half of heaven—stretching from the equinoctial line to the other, antarctic pole, which we cannot see—the left side of heaven.

--- Page 101 ---
<meta>This page continues Filone’s explanation of the universe as a "perfect animal," specifically addressing the six directional dimensions (up, down, front, back, right, left) as applied to the cosmos, contrasting the theories of Pythagoras and Aristotle.</meta>

-># SECOND DIALOGUE<-

[per]fect <note>Completing the word "perfetto" from the previous page.</note> animal—that is, front and back (which are face and shoulders) and above and below (which are head and feet). In an animal, all these six parts are found to be distinct and different. The right and the left presuppose the other four, without which they could not exist; for the right and the left are parts of the width of the animal's body, while the above and the below—that is, head and feet—are parts of the length, which naturally precedes width. The front and the back—that is, face and shoulders—are parts of the depth of the animal's body, which is the foundation of length and width.

Thus, if there are a right and a left side in the heavens, as **Pythagoras** says, the other four parts of the other two dimensions must also be found in it: head and feet from the length, and face and shoulders from the depth. **Aristotle** says that the right side of the heavens is not our pole <note>The North Pole</note>, nor is the left the other pole, as Pythagoras claimed; for the difference and the superiority of one over the other would not be in the heavens themselves, but only in appearance to us, or in relation to us. And perhaps in the other part unknown to us, more fixed stars are found in the heavens and more habitations on the earth; and in our times, the experience of the navigation of the **Portuguese** and the **Spanish** <note>A reference to the Age of Discovery and the exploration of the Southern Hemisphere</note> has demonstrated a part of this. 

Hence he [Aristotle] says that the East is the right side of the heavens, and the West is the left. He posits that the entire body of the heavens is an animal whose head is the **Antarctic pole** <note>The South Pole</note>—hidden from us—and whose feet are the **Arctic pole** toward the **North** <note>original: "tramontana"</note>. In this way, the right side remains in the East and the left in the West; and the face is that part which goes from East to West; and the shoulders, or the back...

*   **Melancholy**, which is cold and dry, having the quality of **earth**.

<margin>The intention the poets had in the explanations of their fables; the Literal sense</margin>

<margin>Examples to distinguish the aforementioned senses</margin>
Perseus, the son of Jupiter, according to poetic fiction killed the Gorgon, and as victor flew into the ether, which is the highest part of heaven. **Morally**, Perseus also signifies the prudent man, the son of Jupiter, endowed with his virtues, who, by killing the low and earthly vice signified by the Gorgon, rose to the heaven of virtue. It further signifies, **allegorically** first, that the human mind (the daughter of Jupiter), by killing and conquering the earthliness of the "Gorgonic" nature, ascended to understand celestial, high, and eternal things; it is in this speculation <note>In this context, "speculation" refers to deep intellectual contemplation or "seeing" with the mind.</note> that human perfection consists. This allegory is **natural**, because man belongs to the realm of natural things.

<margin>
The reason why the Poets did not explain their doctrine freely, but always told fables under various figures.
</margin>

**FI.** They wished to say these things with such artifice and brevity for many reasons. First, because they considered it offensive to nature and to divinity to manifest her excellent secrets to every man. In this, they were certainly right; because explaining true and profound science too much is to hand it over to those unfit for it, in whose minds it becomes spoiled and adulterated—just as good wine does in a bad vessel. From this "adultery" follows a universal corruption of doctrines among all men, and it corrupts further every hour as it passes from one unfit wit to another. This infirmity derives from manifesting scientific matters too openly. In our own time, due to the "broad speaking" of the moderns, it has become so contagious that one can hardly find any **intellectual wine** <note>A metaphor for pure, unadulterated wisdom or philosophical truth.</note> that is drinkable and not spoiled. ...unless they have within themselves an intellect suited to divine and intellectual things, and a mind that preserves true sciences <note>original: "scientie"; referring to structured fields of knowledge or wisdom.</note> and does not corrupt them. **SO.** I like this reasoning: that high and excellent things must be entrusted to capable and clear intellects, and in those who are not such, they are debased. But tell me the other reasons for poetic fictions <term>poetic fictions</term> <note>original: "figmenti poetici"; imaginative stories or allegories used by poets to convey deeper truths.</note>. **FI.** They did it for four other reasons. The first—which is the second overall—is the desire for brevity, so that many meanings <note>original: "sententie"; maxims, opinions, or doctrinal points.</note> might be folded into a few words. This brevity is very useful for preserving things in the memory, especially when done with such artifice that, by remembering a historical narrative <term>historical narrative</term> <note>original: "caso historiografo"; here referring to the literal plot or "history" of the fable.</note>, one might remember all the doctrinal senses included within it under those words. The third is to mix the delightful—both historical and fabulous—with the true intellectual meaning, and the easy with the difficult. In this way, human fragility being first enticed by the delight and ease of the fable, the truth of science might enter the mind with shrewdness. This is just as children are usually taught in matters of discipline and virtue, beginning with the easiest things; especially since everything can exist together, the one in the outer shell <note>original: "forza"; literally "strength" or "outer form," contrasted here with the inner core.</note> and the other in the marrow <term>marrow</term> <note>original: "medola"; the inner, essential meaning or spiritual core of a text.</note>, as is found in poetic fictions. The fourth is for the preservation of intellectual things, so that they do not become changed over the course of time in the various minds of men; because by placing such meanings under these histories, they cannot be altered from the terms of the stories. Furthermore, for even greater preservation, they have expressed the history in weighty and most strictly observed verses <term>weighty verses</term> <note>original: "uersi ponderosi"; poetry written in rigorous meter which resists changes to the wording.</note>, so that they cannot easily be corrupted. For a weighty measure cannot tolerate a defect; thus, neither the indisposition of minds nor the inaccuracy of scribes <insert>writers</insert>...

Joined to this is another goal: namely, that since these poems are a common food for every sort of person, they are a means for knowledge to be preserved <note>original: "perpetuato"; made perpetual or lasting.</note> in the memory of the masses. Very difficult things are tasted by only a few, and the memory of those few can soon be lost if an age occurs that causes men to deviate from learning—as we have seen in some regions and religions, such as among the Greeks and the Arabs. Having once been most learned, they have almost entirely lost their science; and it was once this way in Italy during the time of the Greeks, and only later was the little that exists today renewed. The remedy for this danger is the artifice of placing the sciences beneath fabulous and historical songs <note>original: "cantici fabulosi, et historiografi"</note>, which, through their delight and the sweetness of the verse, are always carried and preserved in the mouths of the common people: men, women, and children. **SO.** I like all these reasons for poetic fictions <term>poetic fictions</term> <note>original: "figmenti poetici"; the use of myths or allegories to hide deeper truths.</note>. It is not, therefore, strange to attribute divinity to the *Ideas* of things; hence they even placed divinity in plants, especially in those that are the most common and useful foods for humans, such as *Ceres* <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture and grain.</note> for grain, and *Bacchus* <note>The god of wine and festivities.</note> for wine, because of the universal utility and necessity that men have for them. Because, beyond the fact that the former [virtues] through their excellence and the latter [vices] through their force participate somewhat in divinity, the principal cause is that every one of the virtues, every one of the vices, and every one of the human passions in general has its own *Idea*. Through participation in these, they are found more or less intensely or weakly within men; and for this reason, among the gods are named *Fame*, *Love*, *Grace*, *Desire*, *Pleasure*, *Strife*, *Toil*, *Envy*, *Fraud*, *Stubbornness*, *Misery*, and many others of this sort. Since each one has its own *Idea* and <term>incorporeal principle</term> <note>A non-physical source or origin point for a concept.</note>, as I have told you, it is for this reason called a god or goddess.

<margin>The meaning of the generation of Demogorgon</margin>

**FI.** It signifies the generation, or rather the production, of all things from the supreme God, the Creator. They say that **Eternity** was his companion because He alone is the true eternal, since He is, was, and will always be the beginning and cause of all things, without there being any temporal succession in Him. They also give Him **Chaos** as an eternal companion, which is—as **Ovid** declares—the common matter, mixed and confused, of all things. The ancients considered this co-eternal with God; from this matter, when it pleased Him, He generated all created things as the true father of all. Thus, matter is the common mother to every generated thing. In this way, these [philosophers] establish only two eternal and ungenerated parents of all things: one the father and the other the mother. However, they established the father as the principal cause, and **Chaos** as the accessory and accompanying cause. **Plato** seems to have felt the same way in the *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato's dialogues that discusses the nature of the physical world and cosmogony</note> concerning the new generation of things produced by the supreme God out of eternal and confused matter. *heaven there is no discord nor any contrariety, according to the **Peripatetics** <note>the followers of Aristotle, who believed the heavens were made of a perfect, unchanging fifth element</note>, and therefore the celestial bodies are not corruptible, but only the inferior ones <note>objects on Earth</note>, because there is contrariety among them, for contrariety is the cause of corruption. And by its being cast from heaven to earth, it is understood that heaven is the cause of all inferior contrarieties, and yet it is itself without contrariety.* **SO.** *How then can it cause it?* **PH.**
*Through the contrariety of the effects of the planets, stars, and celestial signs, and through the contrariety of the celestial motions—one from the east to the west, the other from the west to the east, one toward the north, the other toward the south—and also through the contrariety of the placement of the inferior bodies situated within the roundness of the sphere of the moon: for those nearest to the circumference*

For fire is found only in the bright bodies* <note>the stars and planets</note>*, and water only in the transparent ones* <note>the celestial spheres</note>*, so that even if **Strife**, at the beginning of the production from the womb of **Chaos**, wished to ascend into heaven, it was nevertheless cast into the lower world, where its habitation is today. Whence follows the fable, that being even in this...*

# D I A L O G O

From the birth of Strife, Chaos—burdened with sweats and fiery sighs—followed the hand of Demogorgon <note>Demogorgon was viewed by late medieval and Renaissance mythographers as the primordial creator god or the soul of the earth.</note> and drew from its womb Pan along with the three sister Fates. Understand by those labors in the birth of Strife the natures of the four contrary elements; and by the heaviness understand the Earth, which is the heaviest; and by the sweat, Water; and by the fiery sighs, Air and Fire. And as both the cause and the remedy for the exhaustion caused by these contraries, divine power produced from Chaos a second son, Pan—which in Greek signifies "All" <note>original: "Pan, che in greco significa tutto"</note>—by whom he means the **universal nature** <term>universal nature: the governing force that maintains the order and laws of the physical world</term> that organizes all things produced from Chaos, and that which pacifies the contraries and brings them into agreement. 

<margin>meaning of the name Pan</margin>

Thus Pan was born after Strife, for concord follows discord and comes after it. He also produced with him the three sister Fates <note>original: "Parche"</note> called Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, whom Seneca calls the *Fata* <note>original: "fate"; referring to the Roman personifications of destiny.</note>. By these he means the three orders of temporal things: the present, the future, and the past, which he says God made followers of universal nature. 

<margin>meanings of the names of the 3 Fates</margin>

For **Clotho** is interpreted as the "turning" <note>original: "uolutione"</note> of present things, and she is the Fate who twists the thread that is being spun in the present moment. **Lachesis** is interpreted as "extension," which is the production of the future, and she is that Fate who attends to the thread that remains to be spun upon the distaff <term>distaff: a tool used in spinning to hold the unspun fibers</term>. **Atropos** is interpreted as "without return," which is the past, because it cannot be brought back; she is the Fate who has already spun the thread now gathered on the spindle. And they are called *Parcae* <note>original: "Parche"</note> by way of their opposite, for they "spare" no one <note>This is a classic etymological pun: the Latin word "Parcae" (Fates) was jokingly said to derive from "parcere" (to spare) because they do *not* spare anyone.</note>. He says of Pan that he was placed upon his throne by the command of Demogorgon, because nature exercises the divine order and its administration over all things. Then follows the generation...

Finally, from the father’s side, he gives the divinity of the soul, and from the mother’s side, the ugliness and ruin of the body; for this reason, he signifies poverty, death, burial, and things hidden under the ground, lacking outward appearance and physical ornament. This is why the poets feign that Saturn ate all his male children but not the females, because he destroys all individuals <note>Referring to the passage of time which consumes all living things.</note>, yet preserves the earthly roots—their mothers. Thus, he was rightly called the son of Heaven and Earth.* **SOFIA:** *And who was the son of Saturn?* **FILONE:** *The poets attribute many sons and daughters to Saturn, such as Cronos <note>original: "Cronos," from the Greek word for Time (Chronos).</note>, which means a determined length of time, or a temporal cycle, just as the year is the time of the Sun's cycle. They say the year is the son of Saturn because the longest temporal cycle a person can see in their life—the one that takes the most time—is the cycle of Saturn, which, as I have said, is completed in thirty years <note>Saturn's actual orbital period is approximately 29.5 Earth years.</note>, whereas the cycles of the other planets are completed in a shorter time.* **SOFIA:** *Who was the wife of Saturn and the mother of Cronos?*

**FILONE:** Once, the story goes that **Jupiter**, after he had freed his father from the prison of the Titans, took the kingdom from him and made him flee into Italy. The author is playing on the Latin *inferus*, meaning "lower."</note>, both because at that time it was lower than Crete—so much so that the King [Jupiter] considered it Hell compared to his own kingdom—and because, in effect, Italy is lower than Greece by being further west, for the east is superior to the west. But the allegory is this: when Jupiter is more powerful than Saturn in any person or action, he takes the dominion of that person away from Saturn and makes him remain inferior in influence. It also signifies, in a universal sense, that while Saturn reigns first in the mode of generation <note>The process of creation or biological beginning.</note>—preserving the seeds under the earth and congealing the seed in the beginning of the conception of animals—it is nonetheless Jupiter who reigns during the time of growth and the ornamentation of created things. Jupiter is the principal in this stage; by removing his father Saturn from dominion, he confines him to "hell"—that is, to the dark places where the seeds of things are hidden at the start of generation, over which seeds Saturn holds proper dominion.

Wherefore in the sacred account of creation it is told that after things were created on the first day, the night and the day were created on the second day, and the ethereal firmament was stretched out, which was the division of the air, the water, and the earth. They mean to say that the natural heat of man and animals is the son of Jupiter and Juno because <gloss>because</gloss> it has something of the celestial mixed with materiality. Through its participation in Jupiter and the heavens, it is the subject of the <term>natural, animal, and vital virtues</term> <note>The three systems of the body in Galenic medicine: the natural (nutrition/liver), the vital (spirit/heart), and the animal (sensation/brain).</note>. However, by reason of the mixture it has with matter, it is not eternal like the effective heat of the Sun and other celestial bodies; nor is it always powerful, nor is it always found in one consistent state in the human body. Rather, like a lame man, it grows and then wanes, rises and then falls, according to the diversity of age and the dispositions of the man. And this is why it is said that, because he was lame, he was cast from heaven; for heat and other celestial things are uniform and do not "limp" or falter like inferior, earthly things. He was nurtured by <term>Thetis</term>, who is the sea, because in this way...

When princes are angry with these men for their thefts, they liberate themselves from that anger with Mercurial cunning, removing the causes that could lead to punishment; and by mitigating the fury of the lords, they remain in their favor. Thus says Plato: power and wisdom ought to embrace one another, because wisdom tempers power, and power favors wisdom. <meta>This page continues Filone’s explanation of the relationship between spiritual beings (Intelligences) and the physical universe. ->### SECOND BOOK ###<-

**...of a human individual: the perfection of one of its parts, such as the eye or the hand, consists not only nor primarily in having a beautiful eye or a beautiful hand, nor in the eye seeing much, nor even in the hand performing many arts, but first and primarily it consists in the eye seeing and the hand doing what is fitting for the good of the whole person.** It becomes more noble and excellent through the right service it performs for the whole person, because its own beauty is its own act: hence many times, to save the whole person, the part naturally presents and exposes itself to its own danger, as the arm usually does, presenting itself to the sword for the salvation of the head.

This law being, then, always observed in the universe, the <term>intelligence</term> <note>original: "intelligentia." In Renaissance philosophy, "Intelligences" were spiritual, angelic beings that guided the motion of the planets and stars.</note> finds greater happiness in moving the celestial sphere—which is an act necessary for the existence of the whole, even if it is an external and corporeal act—than in its own essential, internal understanding, which is its own proper act. And this is what **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher whose ideas about the "Unmoved Mover" and the structure of the heavens dominated science during this period.</note> means by saying that the intelligence moves for a higher and more excellent end, which is **God**, following its order in the universe; so that by loving and moving its sphere, it binds together the union of the universe, through which it properly attains the love, the union, and the divine grace that gives life to the world, which is its ultimate end and desired happiness.

**SO.** I like this, and I believe that for that same reason, the spiritual, intellectual souls of men are linked to a body as fragile as the human one: to achieve the divine order in the linking and union of the whole universe.

**FI.** You have spoken well, and so it is the truth; for our souls being spiritual and intellectual, [they receive] no benefit from corporeal society...

*...[concerning things] fragile and corruptible, it might occur to them <note>Referring to the "Intelligences" or spiritual beings mentioned on the previous page.</note> that they would be much better off staying with their own intrinsic and pure intellectual act; but they apply themselves to our body only for the love and service of the supreme Creator of the world. It succeeds in uniting with the supreme God after its separation from the body, and this is its ultimate happiness.* 

*But if the soul errs in such administration <note>The "administration" refers to the soul’s duty to govern the physical body and its desires according to reason rather than instinct.</note>, it lacks this love and this divine union. **FI.** *May God grant it. But you already know, Sofia, that this cannot be done without love.* 

**SO.** *Truly, love in the world is not only common to everything, but is also supremely necessary, since no one can be blessed without love.* 

**FI.** *Not only...*

->## SECOND ##<-

*...conjecture of arguments. I tell you that my love is true, but that it is sterile, since it cannot produce its like in you; and it is enough to bind me, but not to bind you.*

**SO.** *How can that be? Does love not have the nature of a magnet* <note>original: "calamita"</note>, *which unites diverse things, brings the distant close, and attracts the heavy?*

**FI.** *Although love is more attractive than a magnet, nevertheless, one who does not wish to love is much heavier and more resistant than iron.*

**SO.** *You cannot deny that love unites lovers.*

**FI.** *Yes, when both are lovers; but I am only the lover and not the beloved, and you are only the beloved and not the lover; how do you wish for love to unite us?*

**SO.** *Who ever saw a lover not be loved?*

**FI.** *I believe that I am, with you, another Apollo with Daphne.* <note>In Greek mythology, the god Apollo pursued the nymph Daphne, who did not return his love. To escape him, she was transformed into a laurel tree.</note>

**SO.** *So you mean that Cupid has struck you with the golden arrow, and me with the leaden one?* <note>Cupid's golden arrows were said to inspire love, while his leaden arrows caused the heart to remain cold or feel aversion.</note>

**FI.** *I would certainly not wish it so, but I see it is true; because your love is more desired by me than gold, and mine is heavier to you than lead.*

**SO.** *If I were Daphne to you, I would sooner be turned into a Laurel* <note>original: "Lauro"</note> *out of fear of your words than she was out of fear of Apollo's arrows.*

**FI.** *Words have little power, for they cannot accomplish what the rays of the eyes with a single glance usually do—namely, mutual love and reciprocal affection. And so you are always like the green and fragrant Laurel, in whose fruit no other flavor is found but bitter and harsh, mixed with a stinging pungency for those who taste it. So...*
