### D I A L O G U E

...O *Sofia, if your splendid beauty had not entered through my eyes, it could not have pierced my senses and my imagination as deeply as it did. And, penetrating to the very heart, it would not have taken up eternal residence there—as it has in my mind—filling it with the sculpture of your image.* <note>Philo uses the term "sculpture" to suggest that Sofia's image is permanently carved or engraved into his intellect, rather than being a fleeting thought.</note> *For the rays of the Sun do not pass through the celestial bodies or the elements below all the way to the earth as quickly as the image of your beauty passed through me, until it placed itself in the center of my heart, and in the heart of my mind.*

**SO.** *If what you say were true, it would be all the more amazing that, given I have been so intimate with your soul and mistress of your whole being, your "doors" are now barely open enough to see or hear me.*

**PH.** *And if I were asleep, would you still accuse me?*

**SO.** *No, because sleep would excuse you, since it usually takes away the senses.*

**PH.** *The cause that has taken my senses from me excuses me no less.*

**SO.** *What thing could take them away as effectively as sleep, which is half-death?* <note>In the Renaissance, sleep was frequently called "the brother of death" because both states involve a withdrawal from the external world.</note>

**PH.** *Ecstasy, or rather the alienation caused by amorous meditation, which is more than half-death.* <note>In this context, "alienation" is a technical term for the soul being "elsewhere," or separated from the body’s physical functions due to intense focus on the beloved.</note>

**SO.** *How can thought draw a man out of his senses more than sleep, which throws him to the ground like a body without life?*

**PH.** *Sleep causes life rather than taking it away, which amorous ecstasy does not.*

**SO.** *In what way?*

<margin>The value of sleep for mankind.</margin>

**PH.** *Sleep restores us in two ways, and is produced by nature for two ends. One is to quiet the instrument of the senses and the external movements, and to recreate the spirits that perform their operations, so that they do not dissolve and consume themselves through the continuous labor of being awake. The other is to be able to employ the nature of those spirits and natural heat in the digestion of food; for to do this perfectly, nature induces...*

...it unites with the <term>abstract intellect</term> <note>Original: "intelletto astratto." In the philosophy of the period, this refers to pure intelligence that exists entirely apart from physical matter, such as the mind of God.</note> its predecessor, and from there it issues forth again to the corporeal, and afterward returns to the intellectual, according to its occurring inclinations. And therefore Plato said that the soul is composed of "itself" and "the other"; of the invisible and of the visible. And he says that it is a **self-moving number**. <note>Original: "numero se medesimo mouente." This is a classical Platonic/Pythagorean definition of the soul, suggesting that the soul is the first principle of motion and contains mathematical harmony.</note> He means to say that it is not of a uniform nature, as is the pure intellect; rather, it is a "number" of natures; it is neither corporal nor spiritual, and it moves from one to the other continually. And he says that its motion is circular and continuous, not because it moves from place to place corporally, but rather spiritually; and it moves operatively from itself into itself; that is, from its intellectual nature into its corporeal nature, returning afterward into that, thus always circularly.

**SO.** I seem to almost understand this difference that you make in the nature of the soul, but if I were to find some good **example** <note>Original: "essempio."</note> to better quiet my mind, I would be grateful.

**FI.** What better example is there than that of the two celestial Princes, which the immense Creator made as <term>simulacra</term> <note>Refers to a physical image or reflection of a higher, spiritual reality.</note> of the intellect and of the soul?

**SO.** Which are they?

**FI.** The two luminaries: the great one that makes the day, and the small one that serves the night.

**SO.** You mean the sun and the moon?

**FI.** Those.

**SO.** What do they have to do with the intellect and the soul?

**FI.** The sun is the simulacrum of the **divine intellect**, upon which every intellect depends; and the moon is the simulacrum of the **Soul of the World** <note>Original: "anima del mondo." Also known by the Latin "Anima Mundi," this is the concept of an intrinsic connection between all living things on the planet, acting as a bridge between matter and the divine.</note>, from which every soul proceeds.

**SO.** In what way?

**FI.** You know that the created world is divided into the corporeal and the spiritual—that is, the incorporeal.

**SO.** This I know.

**FI.** And you know that the corporeal world is <term>sensible</term>, and the incorporeal is <term>intelligible</term>. <note>Sensible refers to things that can be perceived by the five senses; intelligible refers to things that can only be understood by the mind.</note>

**SO.** This also I know.

**FI.** And you should know that among the five senses, only the ocular sight is that which does all...

Thirdly, because physical quality extends only to a limited space, but light extends through the transparent medium <note>original: "diafano"; referring to substances like air or water that allow light to pass through</note> without limit or measure. Fourthly, because if the producer of a physical quality is removed, some impression of it always remains for a time in the subject—just as the heat remains in water after it is separated from the fire—but when the illuminating source <note>original: "illuminante"</note> is removed, nothing of the light remains in the transparent medium. Fifthly, because a physical quality moves along with its subject, but light, in its role as an illuminator, does not move with the movement of the air or the water in which it resides. Sixthly, many qualities of a single kind in one object become confused and mixed, or rather are joined into one; but many lights do not combine into one. You will see that if you walk with two lamps, they cast two shadows, and if with more, they cast more shadows. Furthermore, if three or more lamps are placed at a small hole from different directions, you will see that they cast three distinct, opposite lights through that hole.

All these things show us that the radiance <note>original: "lume"</note> in the transparent medium, or in the illuminated body, is not a quality or a physical "passion" <note>original: "passiō corporea"; in Renaissance philosophy, a "passion" is an effect produced in a body by an external agent</note>; rather, it is a spiritual act that actualizes the transparent medium by representing the illuminating source. It is separable by the removal of that source, and light "assists" the transparent medium in the same way that the intellect, or the intellectual soul <note>original: "anima intellettiua"</note>, assists the body. This soul has a connection with the body that is either "assisting" or "essential," yet it cannot be mixed into the body's physical matter. For this reason, it does not change when the body changes, nor is it destroyed when the body is destroyed. 

Thus, the true light is the intellectual light, which essentially illuminates both the corporeal and incorporeal worlds. In man, it gives light to the animate functions and to intellectual vision; from this light derives the light of the Sun, which formally and actually illuminates the physical world, and in man gives...

The medium of the other senses is either flesh, as in touch; or vapor, as in smell; or humidity, as in taste; or air that [moves]...

But the eye sees the things that are at the furthest circumference of the world, and in the first heavens, and all bodies distant and near; through light, it encompasses and learns all their species without any passion [suffering]. It knows their distances, their colors, their clarities, their sizes, their figures, their number, their positions, their movements, and everything of this world with many and particular differences—as if the eye were a spy for the intellect, and for all intelligible things. Thus, just as in man (who is a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "piccolo mondo"; the philosophical concept that the human being is a miniature map or reflection of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note>), the eye among all its corporeal parts is like the intellect among all the powers of the soul—an image and follower of it—so in the great world...*

->## D I A L O G U E<-

*eye <note>original: "chio", the end of "occhio" (eye) from the previous page.</note> not only sees with the universal illumination of the <term>diaphanous</term> <note>original: "diafano"; in Renaissance philosophy, this refers to a transparent medium like air or water that allows light to pass through.</note>, but also with the particular illumination of the luminous rays that rise from the eye itself to the object; which rays alone are not sufficient to illuminate the medium and the object; nonetheless, without them, the universal light would not be enough to make vision actual.* **SOPHIA.** *Do you then believe that the eye sees by sending its rays into the object?* **PHILO.** *Yes, I believe it.* **SOPHIA.** *In this you are no longer a <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>A follower of the philosophy of Aristotle, known for his "walking" school of thought.</note>, for Aristotle <note>original: "Arist."</note> rejects it; he holds that vision occurs through the representation of the <term>species</term> <note>original: "specie"; the formal essence or "image" of an object that transmits its likeness to the viewer.</note> of the object in the pupil of the eye, not by sending out rays, as Plato <note>original: "Platone"</note> says.* **PHILO.** *Aristotle did not prove his case against Plato, because I hold that in the act of seeing both things are necessary: both the sending out of rays from the eye to apprehend and illuminate the object, as well as the representation of the species of the object in the pupil; and furthermore, these two contrary movements are not enough for vision without a third and final act; which is for the eye, by means of the rays upon the object, to secondarily conform the received species of the object with the external object itself, and in this third act consists the perfect reason of vision.* **SOPHIA.** *This opinion of yours seems new to me.* **PHILO.** *On the contrary, it is as ancient as truth itself. And what I want to show you is that the eye not only sees, but first illuminates what it sees; so that consequently, you should not believe that the Sun only illuminates without seeing: for of all the senses in the heavens, only that of sight is judged to exist there, and much more perfectly than in man or any other animal.* **SOPHIA.** *How? Do the heavens see as we do?* **PHILO.** *Better than we do.* **SOPHIA.**

How much more could the sight of the great and bright stars do, and especially that of the Sun? ->### BOOK THREE ###<-

->T H I R D<-

**Squares** <note>In astrology, a "square" occurs when two celestial bodies are 90 degrees apart, often considered a position of tension or conflict.</note> occur when exactly half of the Moon's light is in the superior part, and the other half in the inferior. Hence the **astrologers** say that the square is an aspect of partial enmity and is litigious: for since the two contrary parts are equal to one another, and each has an equal share of the light, they litigate over which of them shall take the remainder. And so, when the intellectual light of the soul is equally divided between the superior part of the region—that is, in the **mind**—and the inferior part of **sensuality**, the one litigates with the other as to which of them ought to dominate: whether reason shall rule sensuality, or sensuality shall rule reason. 

**SOFIA.** And what is the significance of there being two quarters? 

**FILONE.** One occurs after the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The "New Moon" phase, where the Moon and Sun are aligned; here representing the soul's union with the Divine Intellect.</note>; from that point, the inferior part begins to surpass the superior in light. So it is in the soul when it moves from union toward <term>opposition</term> <note>The "Full Moon" phase; here representing the soul's total focus on the material world.</note>: after both parts are equal in light, the superior is overcome by the inferior, because **sensuality** conquers **reason**. The other occurs after the opposition: from that point, the superior part (which we do not see) begins to surpass the inferior (which we do see) in light. And so it is in the soul when it moves from opposition toward intellectual union: for after both parts are equal in light, the superior intellectual part begins to surpass and **reason** conquers **sensuality**.

*the superior still prevails, and the inferior is subjected to it. So it is in the soul: when it departs from the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The union of the soul with the divine; astronomically, the New Moon.</note>, it shares a small portion of its light with corporeal things for their necessity, while **reason** nonetheless overcomes **sense**. And therefore, corporeal things are then leaner; for this reason, the **astrologers**, who judge corporeal abundances, say that this is an aspect of "diminishing friendship." The first **trine** aspect <note>An aspect where two planets are 120 degrees apart, generally considered harmonious.</note> of the Moon to the Sun occurs ten days after the conjunction: and the greater part of the light is already directed toward us <note>Referring to the visible side of the moon, representing the physical world.</note>; yet the superior part does not remain stripped of light, but is subject to the inferior. And so it is in the soul when it moves from the first quarter to the **opposition** <note>The Full Moon; the soul’s total focus on the material world.</note>: although reason does not remain without light, it most often operates within corporeal things without conflict. And because corporeal things are then abundant, the astrologers properly call the trine an aspect of "perfect friendship." The second trine of the Moon with the Sun occurs twenty days after the conjunction, following the opposition and before the second **square**: and already the light is being shared with the superior part—which was entirely dark during the opposition—but without conflict. The greater part of the light is still in the inferior part toward us.* 

*So it is in the soul when, from the corporeal realm to which it was entirely dedicated, it comes to give a part of itself back to **reason** and the **intellect**: so much so that, while corporeal things are still more abundant, the **intellectual splendor** joins with them; and this becomes the second aspect of "entire friendship" among the astrologers. The second **sextile** aspect <note>An aspect where two planets are 60 degrees apart.</note> of the Moon with the Sun occurs on the twenty-fifth day from the conjunction, after the second square and before the succeeding conjunction. And in that superior part, it had already re[covered...]* <note>The text cuts off mid-word "recuperata" as indicated by the catchword.</note>

*...superior part, having recovered the greater part of its light, even though a sufficient portion of light remained in the inferior part; yet it is situated in such a way that it is subjected to the superior part without conflict. Although it retains care for corporeal things according to their needs, these remain submitted to the right mind. But because in such a case corporeal things are quite lean <note>In an astrological context, "lean" or "meager" refers to things having little material influence or power.</note>, the **astrologers**, judging them, call this an aspect of **diminished friendship**.*

By the shadow of the Earth, the Moon remains dark on every side—the inferior as well as the superior. It is said to be "eclipsed" because it totally loses light in both halves. *...superior part, but also from the active and corporeal inferior part.* **SO.** *In what way can the corporeal be interposed between the soul and the intellect?* **FI.** *When the soul inclines beyond measure toward material and corporeal things and becomes bogged down in them, it loses reason and intellectual light entirely; for it not only loses **divine union** <note>original: "copulatione diuina." But be that as it may, beastliness, whether in whole or in part, is the highest destruction and the greatest defect of the soul; and for this reason **David** <note>A reference to King David in Psalm 22:20: "Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling [unique one] from the power of the dog."</note> says to God in prayer: "deliver my soul from destruction, and my only one from the power of the dogs."* **SO.** *I am quite pleased by this comparison of the residue of the corrupt, dark, and beastly soul to the eclipsed Moon. Rather, the defect is in us mortals on earth, who, through the interposition of the Moon between it and us, are deprived of its light and remain in darkness.* **SO.** *I understand this; but...*

# THIRD [DIALOGUE]

->THIRD<-

...that you understand me, but you will do me a favor if you explain them. **FIL.**
You first ask whether love is generated <note>original: "generato"; meaning created or brought into being by a cause.</note> and proceeded from another, or truly if it is ungenerated, without ever having had any dependence on any predecessor. You ask, second, when it was born—supposing that it is generated—and whether its succession or dependence was from eternity, or temporal; and if temporal, in what time it was born: whether perhaps it was born at the time of the creation of the world and the production of all things, or instead afterwards in some other time. The third thing you ask is of the place in which it was born, and in which of the three worlds <note>In the Neoplatonic cosmology used by the author, the "three worlds" typically refer to the terrestrial (earthly), the celestial (the spheres of the planets and stars), and the spiritual (the angelic or divine realm).</note> it had its origin: whether in the low and terrestrial world, or in the celestial world, or perhaps in the spiritual world—that is, the angelic and divine. For the fourth, you ask who its parents were: that is, if it had only a father, or only a mother, or truly if it was born of both, and who they were; whether divine, or human, or of another nature; and of them as well, what their genealogy has been. And finally, for the fifth, you wish to know the end <note>Here, "end" refers to the *telos*, or the final purpose.</note> for which it was born into the world, and what necessity caused it to be born; because the final cause <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or goal (the "why") for which a thing is created; in Aristotelian thought, it is the first thing intended by the maker but the last thing achieved.</term> is that for which every produced thing was produced; and the end of the product is the first in the intention of the producer, even if it is the last in its execution. Are these, O Sofia, your five questions concerning the birth of love? **SO.** These they are, certainly. I made the inquiry, but you have amplified it in such a way that you give me good hope for the desired answer; for just as wounds that are well-opened and well-seen are better cured, so too are doubts, when they are well-divided and dissected, more perfectly resolved.

-> ### THIRD [DIALOGUE] <-

<margin>R</margin>

*...desire is entirely different from love, as much from that which is its beginning, which they call <term>complacency: the initial pleasure or resting of the soul in a beautiful object</term> <note>original: "complacentia"</note>, as from that which is its end and goal, which they call joy and delight.*

**SO.** *This distinction seems well-made to me; and you, Filone, why do you not agree with it, but instead posit that love and desire are one and the same thing?*

**FI.** *Once again these theologians, deceived by the diversity of words, seek to impose a diversity of passions in the soul among the common people, which in effect does not exist.*

**SO.** *In what way?*

**FI.** *They posit an essential difference between love and desire, which in substance are the same thing: and they distinguish between the love of a thing that is lacking and that of a thing possessed, even though love is one and the same.*

**SO.** *If you do not deny that love is the <term>complacency: the initial state of being pleased</term> <note>original: "complacentia"</note> in the beloved thing which causes desire, you cannot deny that love is anything other than desire—that is, the principle of it, just as there is a principle of motion.*

**FI.** *The <term>complacency</term> in the beloved thing is not love, but is the cause of love, just as it is the cause of desire. For love is nothing other than the desire for the thing that pleases; hence <term>complacency</term> combined with desire is love, and not without it. Thus love and desire are effectively the same, and both presuppose <term>complacency</term>. And desire, if it is motion, is the motion of the soul toward the desired thing; and likewise love is the motion of the soul toward the beloved thing. And <term>complacency</term> is the principle of this motion called love or desire.*

**SO.** *If love and desire were the same, their opposites would not be different: for the opposite of love is hate, and the opposite of desire is <term>flight: the act of shunning or recoiling</term> <note>original: "fuga"</note>.*

**FI.** *In this too the truth is otherwise: because flight is a contrary bodily motion, not [contrary] to desire...*

<meta>catchword: but</meta>

<summary>Filone argues against the Scholastic distinction between love and desire, claiming they are both the same "motion of the soul" toward a pleasing object. He asserts that "complacency" (the initial pleasure) is the cause of both, rather than love being a separate state from desire.</summary>

## DIALOGUE

*...but of the sequel, which follows desire: because the opposite of desire is <term>abhorrence: a feeling of strong repulsion or loathing</term> <note>original: "abhorritione"</note>, which is one and the same as hatred, which is the opposite of love; so that as they are one and the same, their opposites are also one and the same thing.* **SO.** *I see clearly that love and desire are one in substance, and so are their opposites; but the love for a thing not possessed, and that for a thing possessed, seems—as those people say—quite different.* **FIL.** *It seems so, but they are not different; for the love of a thing possessed is not the delight or the joy of <term>fruition: the enjoyment of the fruits of possession</term>, as they say. In possession, the possessor takes delight and enjoys the thing loved: but to enjoy and to delight is not love; because love, which is motion or the principle of motion, cannot be one and the same thing as joy or delight, which are <term>quietude: a state of rest or stillness</term>, the end, and the limit of motion. I say they have even more contrary paths: for love goes from the lover toward the beloved thing; but joy derives from the beloved thing into the lover. Especially since joy is for what one possesses, and love is always for what is lacking, and is always one and the same as desire.* **SO.** *Yet one loves the thing possessed; that is certainly not lacking.* **FI.** *The present possession is not lacking, but the continuation of its <term>perseverance: the quality of lasting or staying the same</term> in the future is lacking; for one desires and loves that which they presently possess. And the present possession is that which delights, while the future is that which is desired and loved. Thus, the love for a possessed thing is just as much one and the same as desire as is the love for a thing not possessed. But it is something other than delight, just as pain and sadness are something other than hatred and <term>abhorrence</term>; because pain is from the possession of a present evil, and hatred is from not having...*

<summary>Filone argues that love and desire are identical because both represent a movement toward an object, whereas joy is the state of rest once the object is obtained. He explains that "loving" what we already have is actually the desire for that possession to continue into the future.</summary>

*...to possess it in the future.* **SO.** *In what way do you then order these <term>passions of the soul: the various emotions or movements of the mind</term> <note>original: "passioni dell'anima"</note>?* **FI.** *The first is love and the desire for a good thing; its opposite is hatred and <term>abhorrence: a feeling of strong repulsion</term> <note>original: "abhorritione"</note> for a bad thing. Hope follows love and desire, as it concerns a good thing that is in the future or currently separate from us; and fear is its opposite, concerning a bad thing that is in the future or separate. When hope is joined with love or desire, there follows the pursuit of the beloved good thing, just as when fear is joined with hatred and abhorrence, there follows the flight from the hated bad thing. The end goal is joy and <term>delight: the pleasure taken in something</term> <note>original: "diletto"</note> in a good thing that is present and joined to us; its opposite is grief and sadness in a bad thing that is present and joined to us. This passion, which is the last to be realized—namely, joy and delight in a good thing—is actually the first in our intention; for it is in order to achieve joy and delight that one loves, desires, hopes, and pursues. Therefore, it is in joy that the soul finds its peace and rest. And when one possesses that good in the present, one loves and desires it for the future. So, by philosophizing correctly, in whatever way we look at it, love and desire are essentially one and the same thing, even if in our manner of speaking, one type of love is more properly called "desire" and the other more properly "love." Not only these two words, but others as well, express this same thing: for in effect, that which is loved is sometimes <term>affected: to be moved by or drawn toward</term> <note>original: "affetta"</note>, esteemed, opted for, craved, and willed; and likewise, it is desired. All these words, and others like them, although each is more appropriately applied to one kind of love than another, nonetheless in substance they all signify the same—*

<summary>Filone explains the hierarchy of the passions, situating love/desire as the initial movement and joy as the ultimate goal where the soul finds rest. He argues that while terms like love, desire, and will differ in nuance, they all describe the same essential drive toward a perceived good.</summary>

...would be the relative perfection <note>original: "perfettiō relatiua"; Philo distinguishes between God's absolute essence, which is unchangingly perfect, and His "relative" action, which depends on the state of the universe He created.</note> of His divine operation. And I have already told you that the relative divine operation is more perfect when the creatures, for the sake of their own perfection, are united with the Creator than when they are not. But God does not desire His union with the creatures as other lovers do with the persons they love; rather, He desires the union of the creatures with His divinity, so that their perfection, through such union, may be always perfect, and the operation of the Creator related to His creatures may be immaculate. <note>Philo argues that God's "desire" is not a lack in Himself, but a desire for the cosmos to reach its highest state by returning to Him.</note>

->### THIRD DIALOGUE ###<-

**PHILO.** You are mistaken.

**SOPHIA.** How can you deny that everything beautiful is also good?

**PHILO.** I do not deny it, but it is commonly denied by the public.

**SOPHIA.** In what way?

**PHILO.** They say that not every beautiful thing is good, because something that appears beautiful might be bad in its effect; likewise, some things that appear ugly are good.

**SOPHIA.** That argument does not hold. For to someone who sees a thing as beautiful, it also appears good in that aspect where it is beautiful; and if it is truly good in effect, it is truly beautiful in effect. Conversely, that which appears ugly also appears bad in that aspect where it is ugly; and if it is good in effect, then in effect it is not ugly.

**PHILO.** You refute them well. Nevertheless, as I have told you, beauty holds more sway in **appearance**, and goodness holds more sway in **existence** <note>original: "apparentia... esistentia"; Philo is making a distinction between the sensory perception of an object (beauty) and its essential moral or ontological value (goodness).</note>. But in responding to you, I say that although every beautiful thing is good—as you say, whether in being or in appearance—it does not follow that every good thing is beautiful.

**SOPHIA.** What good thing is not beautiful?

**PHILO.** Food, drink that is sweet and healthy <note>original: "poto"; an archaic term for beverage or drink.</note>, a sweet fragrance, a temperate breeze—you would not deny that these are good, yet you would not yet call them "beautiful."

**SOPHIA.** Even if I do not call them beautiful, I believe they are. For if these good things were not beautiful, they would have to be ugly; and for a thing to be both good and ugly seems to me a contradiction.

**PHILO.** I would wish for you to speak more precisely, O Sophia. It is true that "good" and "ugly" cannot coexist in the same aspect of a thing; but it is not true that everything which is not beautiful is necessarily ugly.

**SOPHIA.** What is it then?

**PHILO.** It is neither beautiful nor ugly, as are many things in the category of "good" things. For you see clearly that among human beings—in whom beauty and goodness may coincide—some are found who are neither beautiful nor ugly; and even more so...

**SOPHIA.** What is the adjunct?

**SOPHIA.** What thing is beauty? Does it give an addition to the good, beyond its goodness?

**SOPHIA.** Who does not know the beautiful from the ugly?

# THIRD [DIALOGUE] #

*...is that thing, for which all beautiful things are beautiful: which they call beauty. SOPHIA. Tell me what it is, I pray you. PHILO.*
<margin>Definition of beauty</margin>
*Beauty has been defined in various ways, which I do not think necessary to declare to you at present, nor to discern the true definition from the false, as it is not strictly to our purpose—especially since I believe that further on it will be necessary to speak of beauty more broadly. For now, I will tell you only its true and universal definition. **Beauty is grace** <note>original: "gratia"; in this Neoplatonic context, grace is a spiritual luster or divine radiance that makes a good thing attractive.</note> **that, by delighting the soul through its knowledge, moves it to love.** And that good thing, or person, in which such grace is found, is beautiful. But that good thing in which this grace is not found is neither beautiful nor ugly; it is not beautiful because it lacks grace, but it is not ugly because it does not lack goodness. However, that which lacks both of these things—namely grace and goodness—is not only not beautiful, but is bad and ugly. For between the beautiful and the ugly there is a middle ground <note>Philo argues that something can be "just okay" or "neutral" if it is good but not particularly "graceful" or charming.</note>, but between the good and the bad there is no true middle ground, because the good is **being** and the bad is **privation** <note>original: "priuatione"; Philo follows the philosophical tradition that "evil" or "badness" has no independent existence, but is simply the absence or "privation" of the good that ought to be there.</note>. SOPHIA. Did you not tell me that **potency** <note>original: "potentia"; also translated as potentiality. The state of being able to become something.</note> is the middle between being and privation? PHILO. It is the middle between being that is in **act** <note>original: "atto"; meaning something that is fully realized or currently existing.</note> and perfect, and total privation. But potency is "being" when compared to privation, and it is "privation" when compared to actual being. Hence it is a compositional proportional middle of privation and actual being, just as love is the middle between the beautiful and the ugly. And yet, between being and the privation of that being, no middle ground can fall; for between the **habit** <note>original: "habito"; here meaning a possessed quality or state of being.</note> and the privation of that habit there can be no middle, because they are contradictories <note>In logic, contradictories are "either/or" states (like "alive" or "not alive") with no third option.</note>. For potency is habit in respect to pure privation, and between them no middle falls; and it is privation with respect to the actual habit. And so between them there is no middle, which...*

S 3
<meta>catchword: which</meta>

<summary>Philo defines beauty as a "grace" that moves the soul to love and explains that while there is a neutral state between beauty and ugliness, there is no middle ground between good and evil because evil is merely the absence of being.</summary>

Philo is elaborating on his definition of beauty as "grace," explaining to Sophia why certain "good" things (like food or physical pleasures) are not necessarily "beautiful" because they appeal only to the material senses.</meta>

->D I A L O G U E<-

# D I A L O G U E

*...which is between the beautiful and the ugly; but between the good and the absolute bad, no middle ground exists. SOPHIA. I like this definition, but I would like to know why every good thing does not have this grace. PHILO. In the objects of all the external senses, one finds things that are good, useful, temperate, and delightful; but grace—which delights and moves the soul to its own love (which is called beauty)—is not found in the objects of the three material senses, which are taste, smell, and touch. Wherefore, sweet and healthy food and drink, and sweet fragrance, and life-giving air, and the temperate and most sweet venereal act <note>original: "atto Venereo"; referring to sexual intercourse. Philo argues that while these acts are "good" for survival or health, they lack the spiritual "grace" required to be called "beautiful."</note>, with all their goodness, sweetness, pleasantness, and utility necessary to the life of man and animal, are not, however, beautiful; because in those material objects, grace or beauty is not found. Nor, through these three coarse and material senses, can grace and beauty be conveyed to our soul to delight it or move it to love the beautiful. But beauty is found only in the objects of sight—such as beautiful forms and figures, beautiful paintings, the beautiful order of parts in relation to each other and the whole, beautiful and proportioned instruments, beautiful colors, beautiful and clear light, the beautiful sun, the beautiful moon, beautiful stars, and the beautiful sky. This is because in the object of sight, by virtue of its spirituality, grace is found, which is accustomed to enter through the clear and spiritual eyes to delight and move our soul to love that object which they call beauty. And beauty is also found in the objects of hearing, such as a beautiful oration <note>original: "oratione"; meaning a formal speech or piece of rhetoric.</note>, a beautiful voice, beautiful speech, beautiful singing, beautiful music, beautiful consonance <note>original: "consonantia"; the harmonious sounding of musical notes together.</note>, and beautiful proportion and harmony—in the spirituality of which is found the grace that moves the soul...*

<summary>Philo explains that beauty (or grace) is only perceived by the "spiritual" senses of sight and hearing, while the "material" senses of taste, smell, and touch deal only with physical goodness and utility.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Third Dialogue of Leone Ebreo’s "Dialogues of Love." Philo is concluding his explanation of why beauty (grace) is perceived by the "spiritual" senses (sight and hearing) rather than the "material" senses (taste, smell, touch).</meta>

->T H I R D<-

...but to delight and love, by means of the spiritual sense of hearing; so that in beautiful things which partake of the spiritual and are objects of the spiritual senses, grace and beauty are found. However, in good things that are highly material—and in the objects of the material senses—the grace of beauty is not found; and therefore, though they may be good, they are not beautiful. 

**SO.** Is there perhaps in man any other power that comprehends the beautiful, besides sight and hearing? 

**FI.** Those cognitive powers <note>original: "uirtù conoſcitiue"; referring to the various mental faculties used for processing information and attaining knowledge.</note> which are more spiritual than these know beauty even more than they do. 

**SO.** Which are they? 

**FI.** Imagination and fantasy—which compose, discern, and reflect upon the things of the senses—know many graceful and beautiful acts, duties, and particular instances that move the soul to amorous delight; and indeed, one already speaks of a "beautiful fantasy," a "beautiful thought," or a "beautiful invention." 

And the intellectual reason knows much more of the beautiful, as it understands universal bodily graces and beauties—which are incorruptible—within particular and corruptible bodies. These move the soul even more to delight and love, such as studies, laws, virtues, and human sciences, all of which are called beautiful: a "beautiful study," a "beautiful law," and a "beautiful science." 

But the supreme knowledge of man consists in the abstract mind, which, by contemplating the science of God <note>original: "ſciētia di Dio"; here meaning the divine knowledge or the study of theology and metaphysics.</note> and things abstracted from matter, delights in and falls in love with the highest grace and beauty found in the Creator and Maker of all things, through which it reaches its ultimate happiness. 

So it is that our soul is moved by the grace and beauty that enters spiritually through sight, through hearing, through thought, through reason, and through the mind; because in the objects of these faculties, by virtue of their spirituality, one finds the grace that delights and moves the soul to love.

<summary>Philo explains that beauty is a spiritual grace perceived not only by sight and hearing, but also by higher faculties like imagination, reason, and the abstract mind, ultimately leading to the contemplation of God.</summary>

### THIRD

<meta>catchword: PHI.</meta>

...love cannot exist without a lovable thing or person, but the lovable thing could exist without love—that is, without being loved—and it indeed seems that the lover and the beloved are the principles and causes of love. <term>PHI.</term> What difference in causality does there seem to be to you, O Sophia, between the lover and the beloved thing, and which of the two do you think is the primary cause of love? <term>SO.</term> The lover seems to me to be the active agent, like a father, and the person or thing loved seems to be the recipient, almost like a mother; for according to the words themselves, the "lover" is the one performing the action, and the "beloved" thing is that which is acted upon. Therefore, the lover is the first cause of love, and the beloved is the second. <term>PHI.</term> You know better how to ask a question than how to solve it, O Sophia, for the truth is the exact opposite: the beloved is the active cause that generates love in the soul of the lover, and the lover is the recipient of the beloved’s influence. In this way, the beloved is the true father of the thing called love, generating it within the lover; the lover is the mother who gives birth to love, having been impregnated by the beloved. The lover then brings love forth in the image of the father—for love always ends in the beloved, which was its original generative principle. <note>Philo is using the Aristotelian framework of the four causes to explain a psychological state. In his view, the "beloved" is the trigger that sets the process in motion.</note> Thus, the beloved is the primary active, formal, and final cause of love, acting as its complete father, while the lover is solely the material cause, like a pregnant and birthing mother. <term>formal cause</term> <note>The 'formal cause' is the pattern or definition of a thing, and the 'final cause' is the purpose for which it exists. This refers to a famous passage in Plato's *Symposium* (206b) where the priestess Diotima explains that all humans are "pregnant" and desire to give birth to something lasting in the presence of beauty.</note> and you know that the "beautiful" is the beloved, by whom the loving person is first impregnated, then gives birth to love in the likeness of that beautiful and beloved father, directing love toward that person as its ultimate end. <term>SO.</term> I was in error, and it pleases me to know the truth; but what will you tell me about the meaning of the words, which deceived me? Does "lover" not mean the agent, and "beloved" the patient? <note>original: "amāte patiente." In Renaissance grammar, the "patient" is the recipient of an action. Sophia is confused because the grammar of the word "lover" sounds active, while "beloved" sounds passive.</note>

# DIALOGUE

**PHI.** That is the truth, because the lover is the agent of the service of love, but not of its generation; and the beloved is the recipient of the lover’s service, but not of the causality <note>In this context, Philo distinguishes between the "act of serving" (done by the lover) and the "act of causing the love to exist" (done by the beloved).</note> of love. And I will ask you: which is more worthy, the servant or the one served? The obedient one or the one obeyed? The observer or the observed? You will surely say that these agents are inferior to these recipients of theirs. So it is with the lover toward the beloved: for the lover serves, obeys, and observes the beloved.

**SO.** This holds true in cases where the lovers are less worthy than the beloved; but when the lover is in fact more worthy than the beloved, the judgment should be the opposite: that the lover should be like a father and superior of the love, and the beloved thing like an inferior mother.

**PHI.** Although there are lovers who, according to their nature, are more excellent than the ones they love—such as a husband toward the wife he loves, a father toward his son, a teacher toward his student, and a benefactor toward the one he helps—and more generally, the celestial world toward the earthly, which it loves, and the spiritual toward the corporeal, and finally God toward His creatures, who are loved by Him; nonetheless, every lover, insofar as he is a lover, inclines toward the beloved and adheres to it as an <term>accessory</term> <note>accessory: something that exists only in relation to a more important "principal" thing; here, the lover’s identity is defined by the object of their love.</note> to his principal; for the beloved generates and moves the love, and the lover is moved by it.

**SO.** And how can it be that the superior is inclined toward, and an accessory to, the inferior?

**PHI.** I have already told you that whatever anyone loves and does, they do for their own perfection, joy, or delight. And even though the beloved thing in itself might not be as perfect as the lover, that lover becomes more perfect when he unites the beloved thing with himself—or at least he is left with more joy and delight. ### THIRD

...or the delight which the lover acquires through union with the beloved thing, whether it be in itself more worthy or less worthy, it makes him inclined toward that beloved; but for all that, he does not remain defective or of less dignity or perfection. On the contrary, he remains even greater through the union and perfection of the beloved thing. In this way, not only is one who loves a person inclined toward them for the perfection or joy acquired in their union, but even one who loves not a person, but some other thing, inclines toward it in order to possess it, because of the gain he finds in himself when he acquires it.

**SO.** I understand this, but what would you say when two people have mutual love, and each is equally lover and beloved? You must concede that each of them is both inferior and superior to the other, which would be a contradiction.

**PHI.** It is not a contradiction; rather, it is the truth. Each of them, insofar as they love, is inferior to the other, and insofar as they are loved, is superior.

**SO.** Would each person then be superior to themselves?

**PHI.** Even this is true: every lover is superior to themselves as the beloved. And if perhaps one were to love oneself, that "self-as-beloved" would be superior to that "self-as-lover." I have already told you, when we spoke of the commonality of love, that <term>Aristotle</term> (according to the view of <term>Averroes</term> <note>Averroes: A 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note>) holds that God is the mover of the first <term>diurnal sphere</term> <note>diurnal sphere: In the traditional cosmos, this is the outermost heavenly sphere that rotates around the Earth every twenty-four hours, carrying the other spheres with it.</note> which He moves out of love for something more excellent, just as each of the other <term>intellects</term> <note>intellects: Also known as "Intelligences," these were celestial, non-material beings thought to govern the motion of the planets.</note> moves the other spheres. And since nothing is more excellent than God, but rather everything is inferior to Him, it must be said that God moves that supreme sphere out of love for Himself; and that in God, it is more sublime to be loved by Himself than to love Himself, even though His divine essence consists in the purest unity, as you heard from me more extensively then.

->Therefore<-

<summary>Philo explains the paradox of mutual love, where each person is simultaneously "inferior" as a lover and "superior" as a beloved. He uses the Aristotelian concept of the First Mover to show that even in God, the state of being "beloved" is the highest perfection.</summary>

This does not mean that "nothing" is the matter of things—in the way that wood is the material from which statues are made—but rather that God can make things anew, without any preceding matter.*

*...you indissoluble, because my forces are greater than your fragility.* <note>Philo is quoting or paraphrasing God's address to the created gods/heavens from Plato's Timaeus, where God explains that while they are not immortal by nature, His will keeps them from dissolving.</note> *But I believe that by these words Plato does not mean that the heavens are eternally indissoluble: but it is to show the reason why they are not successively subject to birth and decay <note>original: "generabili, & corruttibili"</note>, nor are they short-lived like the lower bodies, even though they are all made of the same matter, which causes novelty and dissolution. ## DIALOGUE

*...when will they be corrupted?* **FI.** *They say that once the lower world has been corrupted seven times, every seven thousand years, the heavens and everything within them <note>The "pieno" or "plenum" refers to the entire contents of the celestial spheres.</note> come to dissolve, and everything returns to Chaos and primary matter <note>original: "materia prima"</note>. ...which are most clearly preserved in the highest **Ideas** of the **divine intellect** until their new return in the universal creation and generation of the **universe**. *...one to be another, and thus always in continuous succession, all made by an eternal hand, it is more reasonable than the opinion which posits that this world had a beginning and that before it there was nothing. Thus, the strongest arguments against that opinion have no place here—such as the argument that "from nothing, nothing is made" and that <term>primary matter</term> <note>The most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical reality.</note> cannot be newly made or generated. Refers to God as the divine craftsman or architect.</note>, and likewise that the end of His work, which is good, must be eternal. Plato grants both these propositions insofar as they pertain to the divine agent. But he says that God bestows His eternity upon that which is capable of enjoying it—such as the Intellect, in which the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The eternal, perfect patterns or blueprints of all things in the divine mind.</note> reside, and primary matter, which is <term>Chaos</term>. However, their children—who, by means of these two parents, are made and formed by God, such as the whole universe and every one of its parts—are not capable of eternity. *of its intellectual nature: although it compares itself to him infinitely, it is still deficient in the nature of the object* <note>In this context, the "object" refers to God as the focus of the mind's contemplation.</note>. **SO.** *Yes, because it cannot grasp as much as the object is, but not because it makes three out of the pure one.* **FI.** *Rather, being unable to understand the pure unity of the divine object, it multiplies it relatively and reflectively into three; for a clear and simple thing cannot be imprinted upon another less clear than itself, except by multiplying its eminent lucidity into various less clear lights. <meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the eternal nature of divine love. It transitions from the internal "birth" of love within God to how that love serves as the creative force for the physical universe.</meta>

-># THIRD #<-

[eter]nal, because since he is the cause of the birth of the world, it is necessary that the proper and immediate cause be present when the effect is, and the effect be present when the cause is. <note>Philo is arguing that because God is an eternal cause, His creative love and the world's "birth" are tied together in a timeless metaphysical relationship.</note>

**SO.** In what way is love the cause of the birth of the world?

**FI.** The world, like every other thing that is made and generated, is generated by two parents—a father and a mother—from whom it could not be generated except by means of the love of one for the other, which unites them in the <term>generative act</term> <note>The "generative act" here refers to the creative union that brings new existence into being.</note>.

**SO.** Who are these two parents, or progenitors?

**FI.** The first parents are the one God, as I have already told you, and they are the Supreme Beauty, or the <term>Supreme Good</term> <note>original: "sommo buono". Philo identifies God here with the "Form of the Good" described in Plato’s "Republic".</note> (as Plato calls Him), who is the true father, the first Beloved. And the Lover is one with the Divinity, or Wisdom—or perhaps <gloss>division</gloss> <note>original: "divisione". In this Neoplatonic context, this likely refers to the first distinction or "procession" within the unity of God that allows for self-knowledge.</note>—which, knowing its own division, loves and produces the internal love; and the first Mother is one and the same with the Father in that Divinity. Thus, the Divinity, loving its own beauty, desired to produce a son in its own likeness; this desire was the first **extrinsic love** <note>Internal love remains within God; "extrinsic" (external) love is the love God directs outward to create the universe.</note>, that is, the love of God for the produced world. When this love was born, it caused the first production of the first worldly parents, and of the world itself.

**SO.** Whom do you call the other parents of the world?

**FI.** The two first beings generated by God in the creation of the world: namely, the **First Intellect**, in which all the <term>Ideas</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal blueprints or forms of all things that exist in the physical world.</note> of the Supreme Architect shine forth (who is the forming father and the generator of the world), and the **shadowy Chaos**, which consists of the shadows of all those Ideas and contains all their essences (who is the mother of the world). By means of these two, as the first parental instruments, God (as a desiring love) created, formed, and painted the entire world in the likeness of the divine beauty, wisdom, and essence.

<summary>Philo explains that the world was created through a divine "generative act" of love between God (the Father/Supreme Good) and His Wisdom (the Mother), resulting in the First Intellect and Chaos as the world's immediate progenitors.</summary>

-># D I A L O G U E #<-

...and depicted. There was also placed in that creation another **second love** beyond the extrinsic divine love: namely, the love of **Chaos** for the **Intellect**, like that of a wife for her husband, and the reciprocal love of the Intellect for her, like that of a husband for his wife. <note>In this Neoplatonic allegory, Leone Ebreo uses "Chaos" to represent primordial matter or potentiality, and "Intellect" to represent the divine form or mind. Their "marriage" is what allows the physical world to take shape.</note> By means of this love, the world was generated. There was also a **third love** necessary in the creation and being of the world: that is, the love which all its parts have for one another and for the whole, as I have told you at length when we spoke of the <term>unity of love</term> <note>The "unity of love" refers to the cohesive force that holds the diverse elements of the universe together in a single, functioning system.</note>. All these three loves were born when the world was born, or rather when the two first parents were born. 

Therefore, if the world is eternal, as **Aristotle** maintains, these first loves were all born from eternity <note>original: "ab eterno"</note> along with the intrinsic divine love which is one with God—about which nothing more needs be said. But if the world and both its parents were created in a temporal beginning, as we faithful believe, these three first loves were therefore born successively in the beginning of the creation. For in the first beginning was born that desiring love of God for the creation of the world, in the imagination of His beauty and wisdom; and secondarily, once the two first parents were made, their reciprocal love was born, which is the second love; and then, once the whole world was formed with its parts, the third, **unitive love** of the world was born. 

And if perhaps the world were made in time by two eternal parents, as **Plato** posits, that first love of God, which produced the first instruments or parents of the world—namely, the Intellect and Chaos—was born from eternity <note>original: "ab eterno"</note> with those parents. The other two loves, accompanied by the divine, were born at the beginning of time when the world was made. The first of these, that is, the love between the two parents, was born in the beginning...

<summary>Philo describes three levels of love in creation: the divine desire to create, the reciprocal love between Mind and Matter (Intellect and Chaos), and the cohesive love between all parts of the universe. He reconciles these loves with Aristotelian, Platonic, and religious views on whether the world is eternal or created in time.</summary>

*...of the fashioning of the world, the other unitive, at the end of its formation; and as many times as the world was made, just so many times did these two loves then come into being, so that according to the opinion held regarding the generation of the world, the opinions regarding when love was born must necessarily follow. -># D I A L O G U E #<-

...the love that is found in the created world, in which of its parts was it first born: whether in the corruptible, whether in the celestial, or whether in the angelic <note>These three "worlds" represent the Renaissance view of the universe: the "corruptible" is the Earthly realm of change and death; the "celestial" is the realm of the stars and planets; and the "angelic" is the highest spiritual realm of pure mind and intellect.</note>, and in what part of each of those parts? 

**PHILO.** The more distinctly the question is expressed, the less contentious the solution becomes. I answer you that love was first born in the angelic world, and from that, it was shared by the celestial and corruptible worlds. 

**SOPHIA.** What reason moves you to give this judgment? 

**PHILO.** Since love proceeds, as I have told you, from beauty—where beauty is more immense, more ancient, and co-eternal, there love must first have been born. 

**SOPHIA.** It seems you wish to deceive me. 

**PHILO.** In what way? 

**SOPHIA.** Because you tell me that where beauty is, there is love; and yet you have already shown me that love exists where beauty is lacking. 

**PHILO.** I do not deceive you; it is you who deceive yourself. I did not tell you that love *consists* in beauty, but that it *proceeds* from it; and that love is found where the beauty that causes it is present—not that love is in that beauty itself, but in the one who lacks it and desires it. <note>Philo is making a subtle distinction: Love is not a property of the beautiful object itself, but a reaction felt by a subject who looks upon that beauty and realizes they do not possess it.</note> 

**SOPHIA.** Therefore, where beauty is most lacking, there love must most be found, and there it must have been first born. And since the lower world <note>The "lower world" refers to Earth and the material realm.</note> is more deprived of beauty than the celestial and angelic worlds, there must be a greater abundance of love there, and it should be held that it was first born there. 

**PHILO.** Again I find you, O Sophia, more subtle than wise. Just as your memory of things already said serves you to contradict the truth, I would wish that you used it instead to find it. Do you not see that not only does a lack of beauty cause love and the desire for it, but principally when it is pre-known by the lover who lacks it, and judged good, excellent, desirable, and beautiful; then he desires to enjoy...

-># DIALOGUE<-

->I<-

<warning>The first word is truncated from the previous page.</warning>

...wisdom, and every other perfection, that which is found in every created thing is incomparable <note>The speaker is Sophia, responding to Philo's earlier point about God's beauty being the ultimate measure.</note> [to the divine]. But this title of "infinite" that you give to beauty, I do not understand, because "infinity" implies an interminable and imperfect dimension. This is because a "perfect" quantity has its own limits <note>original: "termini"</note> which make it perfect; and if divine beauty is most perfect, it must be complete within its own limits, and not infinite (as you say). This is especially true since "finite" and "infinite" are conditions of quantity—whether extended in space or numbered—which is only found in physical bodies. Since divine beauty is incorporeal <term>incorporeal</term><note>Lacking a physical body or material form.</note> and removed from every physical state, I do not know how it can be called infinite. 

**PHILO** Do not be deceived by the literal property of the word "infinite," which signifies an unending and imperfect quantity. Divine beauty is very far removed from that definition. We simply cannot speak of God, or of incorporeal things, except by using words that are somewhat corporeal; this is because our very language and our speech are, in themselves, physical acts. Even to say "perfect" is an unsuitable <note>original: "incompetente"</note> word for the divinity, because the word literally means "entirely made" <note>Philo is pointing out the etymology of the word "perfect" (from the Latin *perfectus*), which implies a process of making that has been completed.</note>, and in the divinity there is no "making" or "action" <note>original: "fattione"</note> at all. 

However, we use the word "perfect" to mean that which is free from every defect and which contains every perfection. Likewise, we use the word "infinite" to mean that the perfection, wisdom, and beauty of God the Creator is disproportionate and incomparable to any other created perfection. Because He who created every thing from nothing must exceed His creatures (who are nothing of themselves) in perfection by as much as the Supreme Being exceeds pure nothingness. ...absolute privation. **SO.** Give me an example of both. **PH.** In man-made objects, you will see a rough piece of wood which lacks the form and beauty of a **statue of Apollo**; nevertheless, it possesses the **potential** for it. However, a portion of water, just as it is deprived of the form of a statue in **act**, is also deprived of it in **potential**; for one cannot make a statue from water as one can from wood. That first kind of deficiency, which is not stripped of potential, is called simply **deficiency** <note>original: "mancamento"</note>; the other, which lacks both the act and the potential, is called **absolute privation** <note>original: "assoluta priuatione"</note>.

It is the "blank slate" of the universe that allows one substance to turn into another.</term> that is currently in fire or in water—even if it lacks the form and essence of air in **act** <note>original: "in atto"; meaning the state of being currently realized or "actually" existing as that thing.</note>—nevertheless possesses it in **potential**; because fire can be turned into air, and so can water. Nevertheless, this matter lacks the form of the stars, the Sun, the Moon, or the celestial realm, not only in **act** but also in **potential**; for prime matter has no potentiality nor any susceptibility to become the heavens or the stars. 

This same difference exists in the deficiency of beauty between the angelic world and the **corruptible** <note>The "corruptible world" is the physical realm where things are born, change, and die, as opposed to the eternal, unchanging celestial realm.</note> world. In the angels, their deficiency is a deficiency in **act** only, but they do not lack it in knowledge and inclination—which is like the potentiality found in prime matter. And just as in that matter the lack of the "act" gives it an inclination and desire for every form of which it is capable, so the angelic knowledge and inclination toward the **highest beauty** (which they lack) gives them the most intense love and the most burning desire. This deficiency is not an absolute privation, because whoever knows and desires what they lack is not entirely deprived of it: for knowledge is a kind of **potential existence** of that which is missing. And so it is with love and desire. But in the lower world...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Sophia and Filone. ->### THIRD ###<-

in life, no one other than Moses has attained it. **SO.** I have sufficiently understood the resolution of the first doubt; I would like you to solve the second for me: how can it be that the angel is in <term>potentiality: the capacity to become or achieve something that is not yet realized</term> through a desiring knowledge for the infinite beauty, which it is impossible for it to acquire in <term>actuality: the state of being fully realized or completed</term>?

**FI.** It is impossible for the finite to become infinite, just as it is impossible for the creature to be made the creator. And because of this, such an acquisition [of infinity] is not found as a potentiality in the souls of the blessed; rather, they are in potentiality to couple and unite themselves with the infinite beauty of God, even though they themselves are finite. In this, the knowledge they have of His immense beauty serves them, and their love and inclination directs them toward it. 

**SO.** How can the infinite be known by the finite? And how can infinite beauty be imprinted upon a finite mind? 

**FI.** This is not strange, because the thing known exists and is imprinted in the knower according to the mode and nature of that knower, and not according to the nature of the thing known. Observe how the entire <term>hemisphere: the visible dome of the sky</term> is seen by the eye and is imprinted in the tiny pupil—not according to its celestial size and nature, but according to what the size and power of the pupil is capable of. In the same way, infinite beauty is imprinted upon the finite angelic or blessed mind, not according to the mode of its own infinity, but according to the finite capacity of the mind that knows it. For the eye of the Eagle sees—and is transformed by—the bright and great Sun directly; not as the Sun is in itself, but as the eye of the Eagle is capable of receiving it. There is another kind of knowledge of the immense divine beauty that is equal to that beauty itself: this is the knowledge that the highest God has of His own supreme beauty. It is as if the Sun, through its own brightness (which is visible), were to see itself.

There is no other difference between these two impressions except that in **prime matter**, all the formal Ideas are impressed as a physical potential, because it is the lowest of all physical things; whereas in the **possible intellect**, they are all impressed as a non-physical, spiritual—that is, intellectual—potential.

According to this successive gradation of the impression of divine beauty, there follows a corresponding love and desire for that beauty within the **intellectual world** <term>intellectual world<gloss>The realm of pure, non-material thought and spiritual essences.</gloss></term>. This moves step by step from the first intelligence down to the human possible intellect, which is the lowest and most humble of the human intellects.

Similarly, in the **corporeal world** <term>corporeal world<gloss>The physical universe composed of matter and bodies.</gloss></term>—where love depends upon the intellect—this process follows gradually from the first and supreme heaven down to **prime matter**. Just as each of the celestial orbs, through that insatiable love they have for divine beauty, moves continuously and circularly without rest in order to participate in and enjoy it more fully, so too does **prime matter**. With an insatiable desire to share in divine beauty by receiving different forms, prime matter moves continuously from form to form in a circular motion of **generation and corruption** <term>generation and corruption<gloss>The natural cycle of birth, growth, decay, and death.</gloss></term> without ever ceasing. ...who, uniting, generated their own kind, and being satisfied, sought the things necessary for the preservation of life. ...Creator; from this division followed the ability to sin, because the serpent was able to deceive the woman once she was divided from the man in the eating from the forbidden tree of the knowledge of good and evil; and the woman also made the man eat of it together with her, and thus they were both included in the sin and in the punishment.

Once the division was made, it immediately places the deception of the serpent, and the sin of Adam and Eve, and their punishment.

The arrangement of the genitals is placed as a remedy for their perishing <note>In Plato's *Symposium*, Zeus moved the genitals to the front so the two halves could reunite through procreation, preventing the race from dying out.</note>, as you have heard. **SO.** Not only does the Platonic fable show itself to be made for some wise significance, but even the Hebrew history—in this first union and then division of man—indicates a desire to signify something about the nature of man other than the literal sense of the story; for I do not truly believe that man and woman at any time existed otherwise than in two separate bodies, as they are now...

**FI.** God made man and woman in such a form that they *could* generate, but man's proper end is not generation, but to find happiness in divine contemplation and in the paradise of God. By doing this, they remained immortal and had no need for generation, because the human essence and species was preserved in them perpetually; and those who are immortal do not need the generation of children of their own kind. Look at the angels, the planets, the stars, and the heavens, which do not generate offspring of their kind. Generation, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Aristotele"; the Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE). Philo refers here to the Aristotelian idea that nature provides reproduction so that mortal individuals can participate in eternity through the continuation of their species.</note> says, was a remedy for mortality. Therefore, as long as man was immortal, he did not generate; but once he was made mortal through sin, he was aided by the generation of his like, to which God gave power, so that in one way or another the human species might not perish.

Here, he introduces a second allegorical interpretation of the "male and female" creation, shifting from a physical or historical reading to a psychological and philosophical one where gender represents parts of the human soul.</meta>

->### DIALOGUE<-

*...I like the first allegorical meaning, and it incites me to challenge the second that you already pointed out: tell it to me then.*

**FI.** *The first man, and every other man of as many as you see, is made—as the scripture says—in the image and likeness of God, male and female.* <note>Reference to Genesis 1:27: "So God created man in his own image... male and female he created them." Philo is interpreting this not as two separate people, but as two principles within every individual.</note>

**SO.** *How is every man both? Every male or every female?*

**FI.** *Every male, or every female.*

**SO.** *How can it be that the female alone is both male and female together?*

**FI.** *Each of them has a perfect and active masculine part, namely the **intellect**, and an imperfect and passive feminine part, namely the **body** and **matter**; hence the divine image is imprinted in matter. For the <term>form</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "form" is the internal principle that gives a thing its identity and essence, often associated with the masculine.</note>, which is the male, is the intellect; and the formed, which is the female, is the body. Therefore, in the beginning, these two parts, masculine and feminine, were in the perfect man whom God made, united with a perfect union, such that the feminine corporeal and sensual part was obedient to and guided by the masculine intellect and reason; hence in man there was no diversity at all, and his life was entirely intellectual.*

*He was placed in the **earthly paradise**, in which were all the beautiful and savory trees, and that of life was the most excellent among them. Just as in the wise intellect—which was that of **Adam**—and in every other perfect person, there are all the eternal cognitions, and the divine cognition above all, in his pure life. God commanded Adam to eat of all these trees of paradise and of that of life, because they would cause him eternal life; for the intellect, through eternal knowledge—especially divine knowledge—becomes immortal and eternal, and comes into its own happiness. But from the **tree of knowledge of good and evil** he should not eat, because it would make him mortal: that is, that he should not divert...*

<summary>Philo explains a psychological allegory of Genesis, where the "male" represents the intellect and the "female" represents the body and matter. He describes the original state of humanity as a perfect internal harmony where the body was entirely submissive to reason, allowing for a purely intellectual and immortal existence.</summary>

...the intellect toward the acts of sensuality, toward bodily exercise, such as sensual delights and the acquisition of useful things; which are good in appearance, but bad in essence. <note>The author distinguishes between things that seem "good" because they are pleasurable and things that are truly good for the soul.</note> And these are also called trees of the knowledge of good and evil: because in the knowledge of them it is not appropriate to say "true" or "false"—as one does with intellectual and eternal things—but only to say "good" or "bad," according to how they suit the appetite of man. For if one says that the Sun is larger than the Earth, the answer will not be that it is "good" or "bad," but that it is "true" or "false." But in acquiring riches, you will not say "true" or "false," but you will say "good" or "bad." 

Following these bodily knowledges, which divert the intellect from those in which its own happiness consists, is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil that was forbidden to <term>Adam</term> <note>Adam here represents the rational mind or the collective "human" intellect.</note>. This was forbidden because this alone could make him mortal; for just as true and eternal divine things make the intellect divine, true, and eternal like themselves, so sensual, bodily, and corruptible things make it material and corruptible like themselves. 

Yet the Divinity, foreknowing that this way of union between the two parts of man—and the obedience of the feminine corporeal part to the masculine intellectual part—though it brought man happiness and made his essence immortal (which is his intellectual soul), it would instead cause his corporeal and feminine part to decay. This occurs both in the individual—for when the intellect is inflamed with the knowledge and love of eternal and divine things, it abandons the care of the body and lets it perish before its time—and also in the succession of the human species. This is what the text means when it says, *it is not good for man to be alone: let us make him a helper in his presence*, <note>original: "adiutorio in fronte"</note> or rather *against him*: that is, that the feminine sensual part should not be so much a follower of the intellectual part that it does not offer some resistance, attracting the intellect somewhat toward bodily things for the sake of the survival of the individual and the species. 

Wherefore, having shown him all the animals, and recognizing in all of them how each was inclined toward bodily sustenance and the procreation of their like, man began to find himself lacking, because he did not yet have a similar cause and inclination toward the corporeal feminine part; and in this, he desired to imitate the animals. Then, as the text says, God allowing sleep to take <term>Adam</term> <note>In this philosophical context, Adam represents the pure, wakeful state of the human intellect.</note>, and while he was sleeping, He divided the feminine part from the masculine, which from then on he recognized as a wife separate from himself. 

This means that a sleep came upon him that was not ordinary, which is the privation and rest from that first intellectual vigilance and from that burning <term>contemplation</term> <note>A state of deep, focused meditation on divine or eternal truths.</note>; the intellect began to incline toward the bodily part, like a husband to a wife, and to have a moderated care for its sustenance—treating it as if it were his own part—and for the succession of his like, for the sustenance of the species. Thus, the division between the masculine and feminine halves was for a good purpose.

**Fi.** *Once the allegorical intention of the Mosaic narrative <note>The "Mosaic narrative" refers to the biblical account in Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note> concerning the first generation of man is understood, it will be easy to see the intent of the Platonic fable. He says that men were originally double, half-male and half-female, united in one body. That is, the intellectual part and the corporeal sensuality were united in man according to the original intent of his creation, so that the feminine corporeal part was entirely subject to the masculine intellectual part, without any division or resistance. He says that the masculine nature comes from the Sun, and the feminine from the Earth, and the complete Androgyne, composed of both, comes from the Moon. This is because (as I have told you) the Sun is a simulacrum <term>simulacrum: a physical likeness or representation of an idea</term> of the intellect, the Earth of the corporeal part, and the Moon is a simulacrum of the soul, which contains both the intellectual and the corporeal together. This soul constitutes the entire human essence, just as the Moon contains light shared by the Sun but is also made of dense matter similar to the Earth, as Aristotle <note>Referring to Aristotle’s cosmology, where the moon is the lowest of the celestial bodies and shares some characteristics with the "sublunary" or earthly realm.</note> holds. And he says that because the powers of the Androgyne were excessive, it came to fight against the gods—that is, being entirely drawn back into the intellectual part...*
