In this allegory, Jupiter represents the Divine Creator/God.</note> had their genitals turned toward one another, and being satisfied through coitus and the generation of their like, their division was reintegrated. This signifies that the purpose of the division of their intellectual and corporeal parts was so that, by taking satisfaction in corporeal delights, they might sustain themselves as individuals and generate their like for the perpetual preservation of the species. 

It warns, then, that one must not sin, because every half of the man would then come to be divided again, and each would remain but a quarter of a man. This means that if the intellectual part is not united, but divided by imperfect cognitions and counsels, it remains imperfect and weak by nature; for unity is what makes it vigorous and perfect, and division takes away its perfection and vigor. 

And likewise, the corporeal part is perfect when it is united in seeking what is necessary; but when it is divided in the acquisition of superfluous things and is insatiable for them, it remains imperfect and fragile. In this way, through such a division of each of these parts, man comes to lack not only that first intellectual union of the Androgyne <term>Androgyne: from the Greek 'aner' (man) and 'gyne' (woman), the original dual-natured human in Plato's Symposium</term>, but even that state of being a "half" <note>Being a "half" refers to the standard human condition of being one sex seeking its mate to form a whole.</note> as is required in human life; instead, he remains a half of a half, following a lascivious and sinful life. 

This is what the Platonic fable signifies allegorically; the other details that he writes regarding the manner of dividing and consulting and the like are ornaments of the fable to make it more beautiful and plausible.

*...and Venus, Penia* <note>The personification of Poverty or Want.</note> *being needy, stayed outside to receive some remnant of the gods' feast; and the god Porus* <note>The personification of Resource or Plenty.</note>*, son of Counsel* <note>original: "figliuolo del consiglio." In the myth, Porus is the son of Metis (Wisdom/Counsel).</note>*, drunk on nectar, left the house where he was at the banquet with the others and went into the garden to sleep. This means that as the gods—that is, God, along with the <term>angelic world</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, the realm of pure spiritual intellects.</note>—produced a beauty like their own within the created corporeal world (in which they gathered together with liberal generosity and joy, as if at a birthday banquet for that beauty), the deficiency of <term>potential matter</term> <note>Matter in its raw state, which has the "potential" to receive form but possesses no form of its own.</note> intervened there, desiring to participate in the beautiful forms and the divine and angelic perfections. Porus, the son of Counsel—that is, the <term>influential intellect</term> <note>The active, emanating intelligence that shapes the lower world.</note>—drunk on nectar—that is, full of the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The eternal, divine archetypes of all things.</note> and divine forms—desired to share in the lower world to make it good, even if inclining toward what is lower was a deficiency for him.

And this is what she means when she says he went to sleep in the garden of Jove <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods, representing the World Soul or the governing principle of the universe.</note>: that is, he put his vigilant knowledge to sleep, applying it to the corporeal world of motion and generation, which is the "garden of Jove." For the celestial intellect is the house and palace of Jove, where the banquet is held and the divine nectar is drunk—which is the eternal contemplation and desire for the divine and most beautiful Majesty.

When the intellect, the son of Counsel (who is the Supreme God), wished to participate in the lower world, the poor and needy Penia approached him—that is, the potential of matter, which is desirous of perfection. She became pregnant by him while he was "drunk" with the desire for corporeal perfection, half-asleep in his eternal divine contemplation, and turned somewhat away from it to share perfection...

<meta>This page continues Philo’s interpretation of the myth of the birth of Love from Plato’s "Symposium." # D I A L O G U E #

...nor to the needy matter, and from both of them was born love; for love signifies perfection not in act, but in potential. And thus is the intellect within the generable body, which is a <term>potential form</term> <note>A form that is not yet fully realized or active, but has the capacity to become so.</note> and <term>possible intellect</term> <note>A technical term in Aristotelian philosophy for the human capacity to receive and process knowledge, which is "blank" until it encounters information.</note>; and by being intellect, it knows beautiful things, and by being in potential, it lacks the possession of them and desires actual beauty. 

And this is what she says <note>Referring to Diotima, the wise woman from Plato’s dialogue who teaches Socrates about Love.</note>: that Love is a middle ground between the beautiful and the ugly. This is because the possible intellect and material forms are halfway between pure matter—which is totally formless—and the <term>separate forms</term> <note>Purely spiritual beings or ideas, like angels, that exist independently of physical bodies.</note> and actual angelic intelligences, which are truly beautiful. 

Therefore, Diotima assigns equally to Love the conditions and machinations of its mother—needy, variable, mortal, and imperfect corporeal matter—and the intellectual and perfect conditions of its father, the affluent intellect, Porus. And she portrays Love as <term>philosophizing</term> <note>Literally "loving wisdom."</note> but not yet wise, because the possible intellect desires wisdom and exists in the potential for it, since it is not wise in act like the angelic intellect. 

Thus, Diotima showed in this fable of hers that the possible intellect participates in the <term>agent intellect</term> <note>The higher, "active" intellect (often associated with God or the angelic realm) that illuminates the human mind to make knowledge possible.</note>—whether angelic or divine—and that this potentiality does not come to it from its own intellectual nature (as some believe), but only from the company of needy matter, which is deprived of all act and is pure potential. 

She also taught that the first producer of generated love is created beauty, and its own parents are the knowledge of beauty (which is its father) and the lack of it (which is the mother). For whatever is loved and desired must first be recognized as beautiful, and it must be lacking—or be capable of being lost—so that one desires to preserve it forever.

<summary>Philo explains that Love symbolizes the human "possible intellect," which sits between the perfection of God and the void of matter, driven by a desire for the beauty it lacks. He interprets the myth of Porus and Penia as an allegory for how the mind achieves knowledge by participating in the divine active intellect.</summary>

Nor does the "lack" of this beauty come about because of the company of the needy **Penia**—that is, matter—within the intellect, for in that world no matter is found. Instead, the lack comes from the deficiency that exists in the creature simply by virtue of being a "creature," compared to the supreme perfection of its Creator, or the excellence of His beauty over that of the creature. 

Thus, these parents [Porus and Penia] are specific to the love born of the lower world, at the birth of the **Lower Venus**: that is, the beauty shared among created bodies. They do not apply to the love of the angelic world, which is superior to Porus embraced in the garden of Jove, and is alien to the needy Penia.

...generation of the like: a life and being for which they often strive more than for their own. This is because it seems to them that their own life is already passing away, and that offspring is the part of them that is yet to be; they seek to make their life immortal through a continuous and similar succession. Furthermore, these same ends occur in the human soul, which, being pregnant with beauty, virtue, and intellectual wisdom, always desires to generate similar beauties in virtuous acts and wise <term>habits</term> <note>In this context, "habits" (habiti) refers to "dispositions"—stable qualities of the mind or character acquired through practice, such as knowledge or moral excellence.</note>. And just as the legacy of fathers, when they pass away, consists in and is perpetuated through their children, so the virtues of the soul are perpetuated (even if the individual passes away) through virtuous acts and intellectual habits, which grant them eternity. But I see, this being the case, that everything consists in beauty: since the father is beauty, and the pregnant mother is the exemplary, knowing form of it, and the desired son is the return, through unitive enjoyment, into beauty itself. A key Platonic concept where physical things "share in" or "participate" in a higher, perfect ideal or Form.</note> *are rendered most beautiful. The beauty of **oration** comes from the spiritual beauty that orders and unites many diverse material words into a perfect intellectual union—sharing in a kind of harmonic beauty—so that it can rightly be said to be more beautiful than other corporeal things. Likewise, verses, in which there is intellectual beauty, possess even more of this resonant, harmonic beauty. The beauties of **cognition**, of **reason**, and of the **human mind** clearly precede all corporeal beauty, because these are truly formal and spiritual; they order and unite the many diverse concepts of the soul—both the sensible and the rational—and they furthermore provide and share **doctrinal beauty** within minds that are prepared to receive it. There is also **artificial beauty** in all bodies that are made beautiful through **artifice**.* <note>original: "artificio." This refers to human skill, craft, or artistic creation, as opposed to natural beauty.</note> *Thus, beauty in the entire lower world proceeds from the spiritual mode within the forms, and through these forms into bodies. These forms—or formal beauties—are always abstracted from matter, for they never keep company with deformed matter in a way that would impede their beauty; and therefore...*

<meta>catchword: the</meta>

<summary>Philo argues that beauty is a spiritual force ("form") that gives order to the "ugliness" of raw matter. He ranks light, musical harmony, eloquent speech, and human reason as progressively higher types of beauty because they are more spiritual and less tied to physical substance.</summary>

<keywords>Neo-Platonism, Theory of Forms, Light, Harmony, Oration, Human Reason, Artifice, Sublunary World</keywords>

-># THEORETICAL #<-

<sig>Cc 2</sig>

<meta>catchword: ciali</meta>

*Virtues and wisdom are always beautiful, but* **informed bodies** <note>original: "corpi informati." In Renaissance philosophy, "form" is the spiritual blueprint or essence that gives matter its specific identity. An "informed" body is matter that has been shaped by such a spirit or idea.</note> *are sometimes beautiful and sometimes not, according to whether the **matter** is found to be **obedient** or **resistant** to formal beauty.* <note>Philo is explaining why two things of the same species might look different: matter is "stubborn" and does not always perfectly reflect the perfect spiritual "Form" it is meant to embody.</note> **Sophia:** *I understand how all the natural beauty of the corporeal world derives from the form or forms that inform the bodies within its matter, but I still need to understand where the beauty of **artificial things*** <note>original: "cose artificiali." This refers to anything created by human craft or art, rather than by nature.</note> *depends on, since it does not come from the spiritual or celestial origin of natural forms, nor is it of their number and nature.* **Philo:** *Just as the beauty of natural things derives from natural forms—whether essential or accidental—so the beauty of crafted things derives from **artificial forms**. Thus, the definition of both types of beauty is one and the same, applied to both.* **Sophia:** *And what would their definition be?* **Philo:** **Formal grace**, *which delights and moves the one who perceives it to love. And this formal grace, just as in beautiful natural things it comes from a natural form, so in beautiful crafted things it comes from an artificial form. To recognize that the beauty of crafted bodies comes from the form of the craft, imagine two equal pieces of wood: in one, a most beautiful **Venus** is carved, and in the other, it is not. You will see that the beauty of the Venus does not come from the wood itself, because the other identical piece of wood is not beautiful; so it remains that the artificial form or figure is its beauty, and that which makes it beautiful. And just as the natural forms of bodies derive from an incorporeal and spiritual origin—which is the **Soul of the World**,* <note>original: "anima del mondo." A Neoplatonic concept of an intrinsic spiritual force that animates the entire universe.</note> *and beyond that from the **First and Divine Intellect** in which these two primary sources all forms exist with greater essence, perfection, and beauty than they do in separate physical bodies—so the artificial forms...*

<summary>Philo explains that beauty is a "formal grace" that exists in both nature and art. He argues that beauty does not reside in the physical material (like wood) but in the spiritual or intellectual "form" impressed upon it by a creator.</summary>

<page-num>101</page-num>

-># DIALOGUE #<-

[artifi]cial forms derive from the mind of the human artisan, in which they first exist with greater perfection and beauty than in the beautifully crafted body. Just as by mentally stripping away the corporeality of a beautiful object, nothing remains but the **Idea**, which is in the mind of the artisan; so, by removing the matter from natural beauties, there remain only the **Ideal forms** <note>original: "forme Ideali." In Renaissance Neoplatonism, these are the perfect, non-physical blueprints for everything that exists in the physical world.</note> pre-existing in the **First Intellect** <note>original: "intelletto primo." This refers to the Divine Mind of God, which contains the perfect patterns of all creation.</note>, and from it, in the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "anima del mondo." A spiritual essence that bridges the gap between the divine realm and the physical universe, acting as the force that "breathes" life and shape into raw matter.</note>. 

You will well understand, O **Sophia**, how much more beautiful the Idea of the craft must be when united in the mind of the artisan, than when it is found distributed and dismembered in the body; for every beauty and perfection is increased by union and diminished by division. The parts of the beauty of the statue of <term>Venus</term> <note>original: "Venere." The Roman goddess of beauty. Philo uses her statue as a classic example of how a perfect concept is "broken up" when it is carved into physical material like wood or stone.</note> in the wood are divided each by themselves, which makes its beauty slow and weak compared to that which is in the soul of the artisan. For in the artisan’s soul consists the Idea of art with all its parts folded together in such a way that one favors the other and makes it grow in beauty. 

The beauty of the whole is in each part, and the beauty of each part is in the whole without any division or discrepancy. Thus, whoever could see both would know that art is incomparably more beautiful than the crafted object, being the cause of that crafted beauty. Beauty, in the company of bodies, loses as much of its perfection as the bodies gain. For the more the coarse and ugly body is drawn toward the **form**, the more beautiful the crafted object becomes; and the more the form is pulled and hindered by the body, the less beautiful the resulting crafted work remains. It follows, then, that **form without a body** is most beautiful, just as a **body without form** is most ugly.

And that beauty which is acquired through hearing is an image of the beauty of the Soul of the World, because it consists in concordance, harmony, and order, just as forms exist in that Soul in an ordered union. And just as the order of forms within the Soul of the World beautifies our soul and is understood by it, so the ordering of voices in harmonic song, in meaningful speech <note>original: "sententiosa oratione"; speech that is full of wisdom or significant thought.</note>, or in verse, is understood by our hearing; and through these, it delights our soul because of the harmony and concord by which the soul is shaped by the Soul of the World.

**SO.** I have understood how bodily beauties—both visual and auditory—are images and likenesses of the spiritual beauties of the First Intellect and the Soul of the World; and that just as the eyes and ears are what comprehend the two bodily beauties, so our rational soul...

...beautiful, since all eyes and ears offer themselves to them? **PHILO.** You will see the answer to this, together with the solution to your doubt, if you let me speak. This is because its essence is a latent <note>hidden or dormant</note> figuration of all those spiritual forms, created by an impression made upon it by the World Soul, its exemplary origin. This latent figuration is what <term>Aristotle</term> calls <term>potency</term> <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity for something to happen or be known, even if it is not currently active.</note>, and universal <term>preparation</term> in the intellect, which is capable of receiving and understanding all forms and essences. Therefore, you will recognize that all forms and species do not "jump" from bodies into our soul, because for something to migrate from one subject to another is impossible. Instead, when they are represented through the senses, they cause those same forms and essences—which were already shining within our soul—to shine forth <note>original: "rilucere"; to reflect or radiate brilliance.</note>. <term>Aristotle</term> calls this "shining forth" the act of understanding, and <term>Plato</term> calls it remembrance; but their intention is one and the same, despite their different ways of speaking. Our soul is, therefore, full of formal beauties—indeed, those beauties are its own essence—and if they are hidden within it, this latency does not arise from the intellect’s side (which makes them essential), but from the side of the cognition and union which...

The first face, directed toward the intellect, is the intellectual faculty, with which the soul reasons through universal and spiritual knowledge, extracting the intellectual forms and essences from particular and sensible bodies, always converting the corporeal world into the intellectual. These two faces have contrary or opposite motions: and just as our soul, with its first face or rational knowledge, makes the corporeal incorporeal, so with the second face or sensory knowledge—by approaching the sensed bodies and mixing with them—it contracts the incorporeal into the corporeal.

**Corporeal beauties** are known by our soul in these two modes of knowledge, with both one face and the other: that is, either through the senses and physically, or through reason and intellectually. And according to each of these two ways of knowing corporeal beauty, a corresponding love for them is caused in the soul: that is, through sensory knowledge, **sensual love** is born, and through rational knowledge, **spiritual love**. ### THEORIZATION.

Dd 3

...something of the difference that exists between them regarding the nature of the <term>Ideas</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, these are the eternal, non-physical templates or "Forms" for all things in the physical world.</note>, which both <term>Aristotle</term> and his followers strove to deny. **PHI.** I shall tell you. In short, know that <term>Plato</term> placed within the <term>Ideas</term> all the existences and <term>substances</term> of things, so that in everything created in the corporeal <note>Physical or bodily</note> world, he considers there to be a shadow of <term>substance</term> and <term>essence</term> rather than what could truly be called <term>essence</term> or <term>substance</term>. Thus, he disdains corporeal beauties in themselves, for he says they exist only to show us and lead us to the knowledge of those [Ideas]; in themselves, their beauty is little more than nothing. <term>Aristotle</term> wishes to be more temperate <note>Moderate or balanced</note> in this, for it seems to him that the supreme perfection of the Craftsman <note>Referring to God as the "Artificer" or architect of the world.</note> ought to produce works that are perfect in themselves. Hence, he holds that in the corporeal world and in its parts there exists the proper <term>essence</term> and <term>substance</term> of each thing, and that the <term>Ideal</term> knowledge is not the <term>essences</term> and <term>substances</term> of things, but rather the productive and ordering causes of them. Therefore, he holds that the <term>primary substances</term> are the <term>individuals</term> <note>Known in philosophy as "particulars"—the specific, singular objects we encounter, like a specific person or tree.</note>, and that in each of them the <term>essence</term> of the <term>species</term> <note>The general "type" or category.</note> is preserved. Regarding these <term>species</term>, he does not want the <term>universals</term> <note>General concepts that apply to many things, such as "Humanity" or "Beauty."</note> to be the <term>Ideas</term> (which are the causes of real things), but only intellectual concepts of our rational soul, taken from the <term>substance</term> and <term>essence</term> that is in each of the real <term>individuals</term>. For this reason, he calls those universal concepts <term>secondary substances</term>, being abstracted by our intellect from the first <term>individuals</term>. And he does not want the <term>Ideas</term> to be <term>primary substances</term>, as <term>Plato</term> says, nor even the secondary ones, but the first causes of all corporeal <term>substances</term> and of all their <term>essences</term> composed of <term>matter</term> and <term>form</term>; for he holds that <term>matter</term> and the body enter into the <term>essence</term> and <term>substance</term> of corporeal things, and that in the...

-># DIALOGUE<-

<page-num>112</page-num>

...definition of every <term>essence</term> <note>The intrinsic nature or indispensable quality of something.</note>, which is made through <term>genus</term> and <term>difference</term> <note>In classical logic, a definition identifies a general category (genus) and the specific trait that sets the thing apart (difference).</note>, there enters first matter, or corporeality, or a common material form as the genus, and the special form as the difference. This is because its essence and <term>substance</term> are constituted of both matter and form. And since in the <term>Ideas</term> there is no matter or body, there falls within them—according to him <note>Aristotle</note>—neither essence nor substance. Instead, they are the divine principle upon which all essences and substances depend: that is, the former as primary corporeal effects, and the latter as their spiritual images.

He <note>Aristotle</note> holds, therefore, that the beauties of the corporeal world are true beauties, yet they are caused by and dependent upon the primary <term>Ideal</term> beauties of the first divine <term>Intellect</term>. From this difference between these two <term>theologians</term> <note>Philo refers to these ancient philosophers as "theologians" because they studied the divine origins of the universe.</note> arise all the other differences found between them concerning the Ideas, as well as the greater part of all their theological and natural disagreements.

**SO.** It pleases me to know the difference, and I would also like to know your opinion: which of them do you more closely agree with in this matter?

**PHI.** Even this difference, when you are able to consider it well, you will find it exists more in the application of words than in their meaning—that is, in the way they ought to be used. This concerns what is meant by essence, substance, <term>unity</term>, <term>truth</term>, <term>goodness</term>, <term>beauty</term>, and other similar terms used in the reality of things. Thus, in their core meaning, I follow both of them, for their underlying thought is one and the same. In the use of words, however, perhaps Aristotle is the one to follow, because the more modern philosopher polishes the language more precisely, and is accustomed to assigning words to things more distinctly and subtly.

I will tell you this: Plato, finding that the earliest philosophers of Greece valued no other essences, substances, or beauties than those of the body, and [believing nothing existed] outside of corporeal things...

<summary>Philo explains that the disagreement between Plato and Aristotle regarding Ideas is largely a matter of terminology rather than fundamental truth. He argues that while Aristotle provides a more precise technical vocabulary, both philosophers agree on the divine origin of beauty and essence.</summary>

->THIRD<-

...who thought they were nothing, it was necessary, like a true physician, to cure them with the opposite; showing them that bodies of themselves possess no <term>essence</term> <note>The underlying reality or "whatness" of a thing.</note>, no <term>substance</term>, and no beauty, as is truly the case: nor do they have anything but the shadow of the incorporeal <term>Ideal</term> <note>Relating to the "Ideas" or "Forms"—the perfect, non-physical blueprints of all things in Plato's philosophy.</note> essence and beauty of the mind of the <term>supreme maker</term> <note>The "sommo opifice" refers to God as the architect or creator of the universe.</note> of the world. Aristotle, finding that philosophers were already completely removed from bodies through the doctrine of Plato—estimating that all beauty, essence, and substance was in the Ideas and nothing in the corporeal world—saw that for this reason they became negligent in the knowledge of corporeal things, and in their acts, motions, and natural alterations, and in the causes of their generation and corruption. From such negligence a defect and lack would result in the knowledge abstracted from its spiritual principles, because the great knowledge of effects ultimately leads to the perfect knowledge of their causes. Therefore, it seemed to him the time to temper this extreme, which perhaps in the course of time would come to exceed the Platonic <note>original: "metà" – referring here to the moderation or middle ground established by Plato.</note> limit. And he demonstrated, as I told you, that there are properly in the corporeal world essences and substances produced and caused by the Ideas, and that there are also true beauties in it, though dependent on the purest and most perfect Ideal ones. So it was that Plato was a physician curing a disease with excess <note>Philo argues Plato had to emphasize the spiritual world excessively because people were too focused on the physical.</note>, and Aristotle was a physician preserving the health already induced by the work of Plato, using moderation.

**SO.** I have had no small satisfaction in knowing what "Ideas" mean, and how their existence is necessary, and that even Aristotle does not absolutely deny them, as well as the difference that exists between him and Plato in understanding and speaking of them; and of this I will ask you no more, so as not to take you away from our topic—

...are very distant from the perfection of the cause. And therefore, defects fall into them which do not pre-exist in, nor come from, their causes.

**SO.** On the contrary, it seems that from good causes come good effects, and that effects must be so similar to their causes that through them one may know their causes.

**Fr.** <note>The speaker is Filone, though abbreviated as "Fr." in this transcription.</note> Although a good effect comes from a good <term>cause</term> <note>In this philosophical context, a "cause" is the higher reality or "Idea" that brings a physical thing into being.</note>, the goodness and perfection of the effect are not for that reason equal to those of the cause; and although the effect resembles its cause, it does not equal it in <term>perfective qualities</term> <note>The inherent traits that make a thing "complete" or "perfect" according to its nature.</note>. It is quite true that the perfection of the cause induces in the effect a perfection proportioned to that effect, but not equal to that which causes it: because otherwise the effect would be the cause and not the effect, or the cause would be the effect and not the cause. It is quite true that the effect is just as good and perfect *as an effect* as the cause is *as a cause*: but they are not simply equal in perfection. Rather, the effect falls far short of the perfection of its cause, and for this reason defects are found in it that are not found in the cause.

**SO.** I understand the reasoning, but I would like some example.

**Fr.** You know that the <term>corporeal world</term> <note>The physical universe made of matter.</note> proceeds from the <term>incorporeal</term> <note>The spiritual or intellectual realm that exists without physical form.</note> as a proper effect from its cause and artisan; nevertheless, the corporeal does not contain the perfection of the incorporeal, and you see how much the body lacks compared to the <term>intellect</term> <note>The "Intellect" (Intelletto) here refers to the higher, divine capacity for reason and understanding, which exists beyond the physical body.</note>. And if you find in the body many <term>defects</term> <note>In Neo-Platonic thought, physical properties like "taking up space" or "changing" were considered limitations or "defects" compared to the unchanging divine.</note>, such as dimension, division, and in some, alteration and corruption, you will not therefore judge that these pre-exist in their intellectual causes in a defective manner; rather, you will judge that this exists in the effect solely because of its shortfall from the cause. Likewise, the plurality, division, and diversity found in worldly things—do not believe that they pre-exist...

However, love in him is not for the sake of acquiring perfection, because nothing can be added to him; rather, it is for the sake of acquiring it for the universe, generating it as the son of them both. ### DIALOGUE

The Supreme Beauty produced, or rather generated, the beautiful universe in the likeness of His own beauty; for the goal of love is (as **Plato** says) **birth in beauty** <note>original: "parto in bello." A central concept from Plato's *Symposium*, where love is defined as the desire to procreate and bring forth beautiful things, whether physical children or intellectual works, to achieve a kind of immortality.</note>. Since the universe was thus produced by its supreme creator in the likeness, or rather in the image, of His immense <term>wisdom</term> <note>original: "sapientia." In this philosophical context, wisdom is the divine blueprint or the intellectual "form" used by God to design the world.</note>, the creator's love for this universe was born—not as a love from an imperfect being toward a perfect one, but as a love from a most perfect superior toward a less perfect inferior, like that from a father to a son, or from a cause to its unique effect. 

Wherefore the goal of this love is not to acquire beauty that the lover lacks, nor to delight in union with that beloved, but rather to cause the beloved to acquire the greatest perfection, which they would lack if they did not acquire it through the lover's love. It is also so that this divine lover may delight in the greater beauty which the beloved universe attains through His divine love. This is what happens in all loves of causes toward their four effects <note>Referring to the Aristotelian theory of the four causes (material, formal, efficient, and final) which govern why things exist and how they change.</note>: from superiors to inferiors, from fathers to children, from the teacher to the student, and from all benefactors to those they benefit. Their love is a desire that their inferior reach the highest degree of perfection and beauty; the lover then delights in the union with that beloved, and this delight of the lover in the perfection and beauty of the beloved is the very goal of that lover's love.

**SO.** I already remember you telling me about this distinction regarding this matter: the difference between the love of a superior for an inferior and the love of an inferior for a superior. The meaning was almost the same, even if expressed in different words and different propositions; and I realize that even though the goal of each of these two loves is the lover’s delight in the acquired beauty of the beloved,

*“...that this does not satisfy my question; for I am not asking you about the purpose for which divine love was born—which was born alongside the world when it was produced—but I ask you why the love of the created universe was born, and what its goal is.”* **FILONE:** *“I shall satisfy you well when you wish to hear the rest, for which this necessary preamble was the introduction. This mirrors Plato’s definition of love as "procreation in beauty," applied here to the act of Divine Creation.</note> and generates the Son through that preceding love—then, by acquiring with the Son a second and new love toward him, seeks through this second love to lead this beloved son to his ultimate perfection and the highest possible degree of beauty.”* **SOFIA:** *“I still understand this, and it pleases me much to understand it; nevertheless, it does not yet show me the purpose for which the love of the universe was born. <summary>Filone explains that God's love has two stages: the first produces the universe as a "son" in His likeness, and the second leads that universe toward its ultimate perfection. -># THEORIZING<-

**FILONE:** I am about to tell you, but regarding this, you must first understand what the perfection of the **produced universe** consists of.

**SOFIA:** I have already understood this well; I do not need new instruction on that point. Because the universe—as you have told me—was produced in the image and likeness of **supreme wisdom**, its perfection consists in being a proper **image** <note>original: "simulacro." In this Neoplatonic context, it refers to a physical reflection or representation of a divine ideal.</note> of that wisdom. This is the specific goal of its producer, just as it happens with every **crafted thing**: its perfection consists in being made to resemble the form of the art that exists in the mind of the **craftsman**. This is the craftsman's own goal in the making of that thing, and so it must be for this produced universe.

**FILONE:** It is indeed true that this is the **first perfection** of the produced universe, and the first goal of the supreme **maker** <note>original: "opifice." A term for God as the Great Architect or Artisan of the world.</note> in its production—just as you have rightly compared it to things made by art—namely, that it be as similar as possible to the wisdom of the supreme maker. However, this is not its **ultimate goal** and its ultimate perfection. For just as with every crafted thing—let us say, a **drinking vessel**—its first perfection and goal is to be made properly similar to the form and art in the mind of the craftsman; yet its ultimate goal and perfection is to be employed in its own proper function for which it was made, which is to **drink from it**. 

Of these two, the first perfection is the **goal of the work** <note>original: "fine dell’opera." The successful completion of the object itself.</note>, and the last is the **goal of the thing-worked** <note>original: "fine dell’operato." The purpose or utility for which the object exists.</note>. Likewise, in the produced universe, the first goal of the producer and the first perfection of the universe consists in the perfection of the divine work, it being a proper image of divine wisdom; but its ultimate goal and its ultimate perfection con—

*...are partly corporeal and partly incorporeal. **SOFIA:** *Then there are not many acts that make the universe perfect, but only one, which is understanding.*

**FILONE:** As you already know, in corporeal <note>Physical or bodily things.</note> things, love is distinct from the intellectual intent <note>original: "intentione." In this philosophical context, it refers to the mind’s directed act toward an object.</note>, just as a bodily passion differs from an incorporeal act. However, in intellectual and immaterial essences, these two exist together. Their love is intellectual, and their <term>intellection</term> <note>The act of the mind understanding an object.</note> of the highest things is amorous. They only receive a distinction based on reason, not in a way that is real or essential. Their unitive fruition <note>The state of enjoying a thing by becoming one with it.</note> is the final and most perfect intellection; for the more perfect the intellectual act is, the greater and more perfect is the union between the understanding intellect and the thing being understood.

**SOFIA:** Would this intellectual act then suffice as the ultimate end of the universe and its perfection, without making mention of the other two?

**FILONE:** It does not suffice, because this third act cannot occur except by means of the other two. For (as I have told you), among the different types of knowledge, some are without love and others are with love. Of those that are with love, there is one that precedes the love—and love is the end <note>The goal or purpose.</note> of that knowledge—and there is another which is preceded by love, where knowledge is the end of that love.

**SOFIA:** Remind me of these again, briefly and distinctly.

**FILONE:** Those types of knowledge where love does not occur are of things that are good but not beautiful, and consequently not desired; or perhaps because they are bad and deformed, they are hated; or perhaps because they neither are, nor appear to be, beautiful or deformed, they are neither desired nor abhorred. All other forms of knowledge regarding things that are good and beautiful are either of those things for which love or desire is the end—such as the knowledge of food, which is followed by desire when one has need of it—or of those things which are themselves the end of desire—such as the enjoyment of that food through union. There is no doubt that this is the perfect knowledge of food: that is, the unitive knowledge; and because...

<meta>This page continues Philo’s commentary on the Song of Solomon 1:4. He is explaining why the biblical text shifts between singular and plural pronouns to describe the soul’s relationship with the Divine. The liquid stain mentioned in the transcription does not impede the translation of this section.</meta>

-> ### DIALOGUE ### <-

-> [Signature] d i <-

<meta>Catchword: the</meta>

...are of the same quality as the love of wine, which intoxicates a man and removes him from the <term>rectitude</term> <note>In this context, "rectitude" refers to the "straightness" or moral and rational alignment of the mind with truth.</note> of the mind; therefore, it concludes: *the upright love You.* <note>Song of Solomon 1:4. Philo is contrasting the "crooked" intoxication of wine with the "straight" or "upright" love of God.</note> It means that You are not loved through an unrighteous mind, as is the case with <term>carnal loves</term> <note>Physical or lustful desires as opposed to spiritual or intellectual love.</note>; rather, it is the soul’s own uprightness that loves You.

Notice how he begins by speaking in the singular, saying *draw me*, and immediately shifts to the plural, saying *we will run after You*. He then returns to the singular: *if the King brings me into his chambers*, and shifts again to the plural: *we will delight and rejoice in You; we would remember Your loves more than wine*. This is to show that through the union of the <term>intellectual part</term> <note>The highest faculty of the human soul, which allows it to connect with the divine order.</note> of man—or of the whole created universe—it brings us happiness and delight; not only to the soul itself, but to all parts of the universe along with it.

For this reason, he uses the plural: *the upright love You*, because all things strive toward divine love by means of the intellectual part. Thus, the operation and the radiance of divine love within us is what first guides us toward our blissful delight. Following that comes the most ardent work of our own love within us, which leads us to unite and find bliss in His supreme beauty.

To understand this better, consider the similarity between two perfect lovers, a man and a woman. Although the male lover may feel an ardent love for his beloved, he never has the courage or the possibility of enjoying that delightful union—which is the ultimate goal of his love—unless she, with the rays of her loving eyes, with sweet words, gentle bearing, pleasing signals, and affectionate gestures, shows him such a graciousness of mutual love. This response raises and ignites his love, making him capable and bold enough to lead himself, as a lover, into—

<summary>Philo explains that divine love "uprights" the soul, contrasting it with the "drunkenness" of worldly desire, and uses the metaphor of human courtship to illustrate how God's initial grace encourages the soul's return to Him.</summary>

**SOFIA.** I now have full satisfaction regarding these doubts of mine; and as for the obligation you had to tell me of the birth of love, you are now released from it, having paid me no less a sum than you did previously regarding the essence of love and desire, and afterwards regarding the <term>universality of love</term> <note>The concept that love exists in all levels of being, from the elements to the divine.</note>. I see that the beginning of its birth within the created universe is in the <term>angelic world</term> <note>In Ebreo’s Neoplatonic cosmology, the "angelic world" is the realm of pure intellect that exists between God and the physical world.</note>, and thus I recognize its most noble genealogy. And yet, Philo, I used to believe that the reason love was born was sometimes to afflict and torture lovers who affectionately love their beloveds.

**PHILO.** Although love brings with it affliction and torment, anxiety, and toil, and many other pains which would take long to recount, these are not its proper end; rather, its end is that sweet delight which is the opposite of these. Nevertheless, you have spoken the truth—not regarding all love, but only concerning my love for you. I see that its end has never been pleasure or delight; rather, its beginning, its middle, and its end are entirely...
